Read with its mate, it shows the tight back-and-forth that bound the Union's cause in Britain to two men's pens. The orders it would soon draw back complete the loop.
frus-1863p1-d166:
On 23 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 166 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Adams's pair held the rest of the day's London news, split off for clean filing at home. His April mail is a close chart of Britain's turn on the ship question. This letter is the mate to document 165. Together the pair closes the legation's mail for the week, in the split-sheet habit that marks the whole file.
frus-1863p1-d266:
A dispatch dated 21 August 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 266 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Union wins at Gettysburg and Vicksburg in early July 1863 weakened the case for aiding the South. British leaders grew more careful, and Adams's post grew a little less tense. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d366:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 20 January 1863. It appears as document 366 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d466:
A dispatch dated 17 April 1863 went from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d566:
From Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington: a letter dated 10 June 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d666:
The 17 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020366:
Susan R. Schwab, Jessica A. Shugart, Tiffany Horng, and their team found an odd source of immune targets in PLOS Biology in 2004. The immune system attacks cells that display foreign protein pieces, called antigens. Proteins are normally read starting from an AUG code in the RNA. The team showed some antigens start instead at CUG, with the amino acid leucine.

That nonstandard start means cells display more kinds of pieces than expected. Hidden starts could help explain how the immune system spots some infected or cancerous cells that lack obvious foreign proteins. They also widen the search space for vaccine design. The work is a reminder that the rules for reading genes have more exceptions than textbooks suggest.
plos-pone-0000066:
Ana Carmena, Stephan Speicher, and Mary Baylies studied a linker protein in the fruit fly in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein, Canoe, also called AF-6, has a PDZ domain, a common docking module. The authors show Canoe binds a key protein in the Ras-MAPK pathway and ties three major signal routes together.

Ras-MAPK, Notch, and Wingless/Wnt signals each guide growth and pattern in embryos. A protein that touches all three can coordinate their timing. That kind of coordination is how embryos keep many instructions from clashing. The work adds Canoe to the list of hub proteins worth watching in development and in cancers where Ras signals run hot.
plos-pone-0000166:
Pierre Krystkowiak, Véronique Gaura, Myriam Labalette, and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Patients with Huntington's disease received grafts of foetal neural tissue into the brain, an experimental attempt to replace lost neurons. The authors report that some patients became immunized against donor antigens, leading to immune rejection of the grafts.

The brain was long thought to be partly sheltered from immune attack, but these results show rejection can still happen. The paper documents alloimmunisation in graft recipients and its consequences. For cell transplant therapies in the brain, it underlines that immune matching and monitoring cannot be skipped.
plos-pone-0000266:
Joseph J. Gillespie, Magda S. Beier, M. Sayeedur Rahman, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Rickettsia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause diseases like typhus. The authors use plasmids, small DNA circles, from Rickettsia felis to gain insight into how the whole group evolved.

Plasmids move between bacteria and carry genes that can reshape a genome. Finding them in Rickettsia, long thought to lack them, changes the group's evolutionary story. The paper traces how plasmid genes fit into rickettsial history, with implications for how these pathogens gain new traits.
plos-pone-0000366:
Amir Ali Abbasi and colleagues wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE paper on the human GLI3 gene. The gene helps guide how body parts form as an embryo grows. Much of the DNA inside the gene does not code for protein. The team asked whether some of these stretches act as switches. Those switches would turn genes on in specific tissues.

Their study reports that conserved non-coding stretches inside GLI3 work as enhancers. Enhancers are DNA elements that boost gene activity. These ones act in certain tissues rather than everywhere. Results like these help map the hidden control layer of the genome, where small changes can alter development even when the protein itself is unchanged.
plos-pone-0000466:
Linley E. Watson and colleagues showed how anthrax toxins can cause shock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Anthrax's deadliest phase often involves a sudden collapse of circulation. Working with rats, the team found that anthrax toxins induce shock by depressing cardiac ventricular function, weakening the heart's main pumping chambers.

If the collapse is driven by the heart rather than only by blood vessels, treatment thinking changes. Supporting heart function becomes part of countering the toxin. Mechanistic findings like this matter for biodefense medicine, where the goal is to keep patients alive after exposure long enough for antibiotics to work.
plos-pone-0000566:
Blanca Amengual and colleagues tracked a bat rabies relative through natural colonies over time, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. European bat lyssavirus type 1 is related to rabies and infects bats across Europe. The team studied its temporal dynamics and the survival of Myotis myotis bats in natural colonies.

How a virus persists in a colony without killing it off decides the long-term risk to people and livestock. Following real colonies across seasons shows whether the virus flares, fades, or smolders. Such ecology is the basis for bat conservation that also manages disease risk, rather than reflexive culling.
plos-pone-0000666:
Debbie A. Lawlor, Susan Morton, G. David Batty and colleagues asked whether a doctor's judgment in pregnancy echoes decades later. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study used a birth cohort of 11,106 people, followed for 245,000 person-years in total. Obstetricians had assessed each mother's physical health at the time of pregnancy. The outcome tracked was the children's cardiovascular disease risk as adults.

The title gives the result: the obstetrician's assessment predicts offspring future health. A simple clinical judgment, recorded once, carried signal about the next generation. That raises questions about what such assessments capture, from the mother's condition to her circumstances, and how far their reach extends.
plos-pone-0000766:
Sven Heinicke, Michael S. Livstone, Charles Lu and co-authors built a web database that matches genes across species. Many such databases were already online in 2007. To the authors' knowledge, none of them mixed results from several matching methods with facts checked by hand. Their tool is called P-POD, the Princeton Protein Orthology Database, and it appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.

Orthology means genes in two species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. If a mouse gene is the match of a human gene, what is known in mice may apply to us. P-POD was made for working biologists, not just computer experts. Good matches, backed by hand checks, make cross-species claims safer to use.
plos-pone-0000866:
Najmus Mahfooz, Nataliya Turchyn, Michelle Mihajlovic and co-authors looked at why insect hind legs grow so much larger than other legs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Big hind legs are a hallmark of insect history, yet the steps behind that growth were not known. The team studied the milkweed bug, a species where the third pair of legs is clearly enlarged.

Their work centers on Ubx, a gene that helps give body parts their identity. They trace how Ubx shapes both the extra growth and the varied forms of hind legs. The study links a single gene to a trait seen across many insect groups.
plos-pone-0000966:
Wai-Ming Lee, Christin Kiesner, Tressa Pappas and colleagues identified a set of unrecognized rhinoviruses in sick infants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human rhinoviruses are the most common human pathogens and the usual cause of colds. At the time, one hundred and one types were classed into groups A and B by their sequences.

The team found a diverse group outside that scheme, and show these viruses commonly cause respiratory illness in infants. Illness from rhinoviruses ranges from no symptoms to severe lower airway disease. A missed branch of the family tree means tests built on the old groups may overlook real cases.
plos-pone-0001066:
Daciana Margineantu, Christine Emerson, Dolores Diaz and colleagues found that blocking Hsp90 slows mitochondrial protein turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drugs that inhibit Hsp90, a major chaperone, change cells in many ways. Treated cells expand their mitochondrial compartment, the mitochondria fragment and condense, and in time their integrity fails and the cell dies.

The team focus on protein turnover inside mitochondria under that treatment. A slower turnover could explain the buildup and odd shapes. Hsp90 inhibitors are cancer drug candidates, so their full effects on the cell's power plants matter. Mitochondrial damage may be part of how they kill tumor cells.
plos-pone-0001166:
Malaria in pregnancy is dangerous for mother and child, and drug resistance in Africa has shrunk the treatment options. Linda Kalilani and colleagues ran a pilot trial in Blantyre, Malawi, reported in 2007 in PLOS ONE. They added either azithromycin, an antibiotic, or artesunate, a fast malaria drug, to the standard sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.

The randomized controlled trial tested the safety and the benefit of the two combinations in pregnant women. New regimens are badly needed across sub-Saharan Africa as resistance grows. A pilot trial like this one checks whether a fuller trial is worth doing and how it should be run.
plos-pone-0001266:
Whether scientists disclose their financial ties affects public trust in research. Daniel Cook and colleagues checked how newspapers handle those disclosures, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They searched a news database for the top science stories published in 2004 and 2005 and conducted a content analysis. The database they searched was Lexis/Nexis Academic News.

The authors examined how often the lay press reported conflicts of interest behind the science it covered. Forthright reporting of financial ties is associated with public trust in the scientific enterprise, they note. Their audit measures how far short of that standard popular coverage fell.
plos-pone-0001366:
Corinne Rodgers and her co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2007 on waves of low nerve activity in the locust brain. These waves, called spreading depression, also occur in people. In humans they are linked to stroke, seizures, and migraine. The team asked whether stress before a wave could change how the wave acts.

The authors describe waves like these in a simple model, the nerve cord of the locust. They test how brief stress first changes later waves. The work gives a cheap and clear way to study a brain event that is hard to watch in people. It may help explain why some brains cope with such waves better than others.
plos-pone-0001466:
Gwenn Le Mée and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on toxic RNA repeats in fruit flies. Some human ills grow from RNA with a repeated stretch that turns toxic. One such ill weakens muscle and is tied to harm from these repeats. The team used fly models to test what drives that harm.

They varied both the length of the repeat and how much RNA the flies made. Neither trait alone proved to be the main driver of harm in their tests. That result shifts focus to other traits of the toxic RNA. It refines how labs should model this class of disease in flies.
plos-pone-0001566:
Torsten Ochsenreiter, Michael Cipriano, and Stephen Hajduk published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on RNA editing in trypanosomes. These parasites rewrite their power unit messages by adding or cutting letters. The edits are guided by small RNAs and are vital for the cell's energy work. Most known edits were of the deep, standard kind.

The team found a second, more varied kind of edit is wide spread too. These edits may add to the range of proteins the power units can make. A wider edit map changes the count of what these parasites can do with few genes. It also hints at how RNA editing first arose.
plos-pone-0001666:
Kenichi Yamahara and co-authors tested a combined cell transplant to restore blood flow in legs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In earlier work, the group had grown vascular progenitor cells from embryonic stem cells. Those cells could become both endothelial cells, which line vessels, and mural cells, which wrap and support them.

For this study they derived the matching human cells and transplanted both types together into limbs with poor blood flow, a condition called hindlimb ischemia. The full text gives the cell preparation, the transplant results, and the new vessel growth they measured. Using both cell types at once mimics how vessels form in the body. The approach may one day help patients whose limbs are starved of blood.
plos-pone-0001766:
Xavier Roux, Catherine Dubuquoy, Guillaume Durand, and their co-authors built a nasal vaccine candidate against a baby-threatening virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis in children under two and is a growing public health concern. No safe, effective vaccine existed. The virus's nucleoprotein, a core component, had performed poorly as a vaccine part on its own.

The team packaged the nucleoprotein into sub-nucleocapsid nanoparticles and delivered them through the nose. The full text gives the particle design and the immune results. Nasal delivery suits a virus that enters through airways, and particle packaging can turn a weak antigen into a workable vaccine.
plos-pone-0001866:
Vera Rocha-Perugini, Claire Montpellier, David Delgrange, and their co-authors studied a protein that blocks hepatitis C virus entry in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Two to three percent of the world's population is chronically infected with HCV and at risk of liver cancer. The precise mechanisms regulating HCV entry into liver cells were still unknown, though several cell surface proteins had been identified as needed.

The team reports that EWI-2wint, a partner of the CD81 surface protein, inhibits hepatitis C virus entry. The full text gives the cell infection assays. Entry blockers are attractive drugs because they act before the virus is inside, and each new entry factor refines the target list.
plos-pone-0001966:
Mahan Azadpour and Evan Balaban tested how the brain hears speech-like sounds that are not speech, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Brain scans of speech often use fake speech sounds, and whether each sound counts as speech is set by what listeners say they hear. Brain results are then read through those labels, which can bias the science.

The pair asked whether the brain uses sound patterns from speech, called phonological patterns, without a person being aware of it. They tested this with complex signals that are not speech. If it does, labels based on reports alone are shaky. The study urges more care in how speech scans are designed.
plos-pone-0002066:
Giacomo Donati and co-authors studied a switch that flips gene tags from on to off, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Histone tails carry many chemical tags, placed in unlike ways in open and closed parts of the genome. Two tags mark early active chromatin, and a third marks inactive chromatin, setting up the split between used and unused genes.

The switch centers on NF-Y, a protein bound to promoters with a CCAAT motif. The team report that NF-Y drives a change from positive to negative histone methyl marks on those promoters. Such a flip could be how genes are shut for the long term.
plos-pone-0002166:
Yanjun Li, Erhei Dai, Yujun Cui, and co-authors refined a DNA typing method for the plague bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Yersinia pestis, the germ that causes plague, still circulates in parts of China. The team's method, called different region analysis, sorts strains by which chunks of DNA they carry or lack.

Here they widened the method to 23 such regions and applied it to 909 Chinese strains of the bacterium. The larger test checked whether the typing scheme holds up and what it reveals about how local strains adapt. Reliable typing helps track where plague strains come from and how they move.
plos-pone-0002266:
Olivier Hermine, Olivier Lortholary, Phillip Leventhal, and co-authors surveyed patients with mastocytosis about how the disease disables daily life, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mastocytosis is a rare disease where mast cells build up in tissues. Its mild forms make up over 90 percent of cases, yet how its symptoms affect quality of life had not been well studied.

The team ran a case-control study comparing patients' self-reported disability with that of healthy people. They mapped which symptoms hurt most and how deep the impact runs. For a disease often called mild on paper, measured patient experience gives doctors and regulators a truer picture of its burden.
plos-pone-0002366:
Giovanna Ponti, Paolo Peretto, and Luca Bonfanti looked for new neuron production in the rabbit cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In adult mammals, the birth of new neurons is restricted to a few brain regions, unlike in other vertebrates where it is widespread. In the mammalian cerebellum, new neurons were thought to appear only in the earliest postnatal days.

The team studied peripuberal and adult rabbits, whose cerebellum keeps growing late. They document the genesis of neuronal and glial progenitors in the cerebellar cortex at those ages. A late window of cell birth in a motor center revises the map of where adult brains can still build.
plos-pone-0002466:
In 2008, Skov and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Vibe Skov, Dorte Glintborg, Steen Knudsen, and others. Its subject is pioglitazone Enhances Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Ribosomal Protein Biosynthesis in Skeletal Muscle in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Insulin resistance is a common metabolic abnormality in women with PCOS and leads to an elevated risk of type 2 diabetes.

Studies have shown that thiazolidinediones (TZDs) improve metabolic disturbances in PCOS patients. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002566:
A research team led by Wu reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Dongying Wu, Amber Hartman, Naomi Ward, and others. Its subject is an Automated Phylogenetic Tree-Based S mall Subunit rRNA T axonomy and A lignment P ipeline (STAP). Comparing small-subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences underpins much of what is known about microbial diversity.

That holds for both cultured microbes and microbes that have never been grown in a lab. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002666:
Min Zhao led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was amelioration of Streptozotocin-Induced diabetes in mice with cells derived from human marrow stromal cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Min Zhao and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Pluri-potent bone marrow stromal cells (MSCs) provide an attractive opportunity to generate unlimited glucose-responsive insulin-producing cells for the treatment of diabetes. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002766:
Asma Khalil led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was effect of antihypertensive therapy with alpha methyldopa on levels of angiogenic factors in pregnancies with hypertensive disorders. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Asma Khalil, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Antihypertensive drugs are believed to lower blood pressure in pre-eclampsia by direct or central vasodilatory mechanisms. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002866:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Martin Voss and colleagues addresses mere expectation to move causes attenuation of sensory signals. The catalog record names Martin Voss first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. When a part of the body moves, the sensation evoked by a probe stimulus to that body part is attenuated. The summary also notes a further point. Two mechanisms have been proposed to explain this robust and general effect. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002966:
Vincent Plagnol, Elif Uz, Chris Wallace and co-authors warned in 2008 that many lymphoblastoid cell lines are far less mixed than assumed. These lab-grown lines from blood cells are used widely to study gene expression, including allele-specific work. Earlier results hinted a tenth of human genes show random monoallelic expression.

Extreme clonality means a line descends from very few starting cells, which can skew expression results. The PLOS ONE paper sets out the scale of the problem and its implications. Geneticists using these lines for expression assays need to account for it or risk false patterns.
plos-pone-0003066:
Daouda Sissoko, Amrat Moendandze, Denis Malvy and co-authors surveyed chikungunya infection on Mayotte for 2005 to 2006. Since 2006 the virus had re-emerged as a pathogen of global concern. Individual and household factors behind infection, and the scale of silent infections, remained poorly understood.

Their population-based survey measured seroprevalence, the share with antibodies, and risk factors on the island. Published in PLOS ONE, knowing how many infections passed silently changes outbreak counts and control plans. Household data show where transmission concentrates. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003166:
Joseph Donroe, Monica Tincopa, Robert H. Gilman and colleagues study child pedestrian injuries in urban Peru in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Road traffic injuries to child pedestrians are an important cause of death and disability in poorer nations. Yet prevention there largely draws on studies from wealthier countries, which may not fit local streets and habits.

Using case-control analyses, the team investigate personal and environmental risk factors for these injuries in children and adolescents. Readers get evidence gathered where the burden actually falls. Local data like this can shape safer routes, traffic rules, and school area design that imported advice might miss.
plos-pone-0003266:
Junya Hirokawa, Akiya Watakabe, Sonoko Ohsawa and colleagues map gene patterns across rat cortex in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The mammalian neocortex is subdivided into many areas, each of which exhibits distinctive lamina architecture. To investigate such area differences in detail, the team chose three genes for comparative analyses, namely RORbeta, ER81 and Nurr1, whose messages had been reported as area markers.

Using double in situ hybridization and a cortical box method, they analyse area-specific expression patterns. Readers get a finer map of how cortex areas differ in gene use. Such maps help link anatomy to function in the brain's outer layer.
plos-pone-0003366:
Rosalynn L. Ord, Adriana Tami and Colin J. Sutherland compare malaria parasite genes in Venezuela in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The authors present the first population genetic analysis of homologous loci. The loci come from two sympatric human malaria parasite groups sharing the same human hosts. They use full-length sequences of ama1 genes from Plasmodium vivax and P. falciparum. The samples were collected in the Venezuelan Amazon.

The title reports ama1 genes of the two species differ sharply in genetic diversity and recombination rate. Readers see two parasites in one place evolve by different rules. The ama1 gene is a vaccine candidate, so its diversity directly affects vaccine design.
plos-pone-0007466:
Leticia Olvera and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how E. coli manages its core metabolism when sugar runs short. The bacterium normally imports glucose through a transport system called the PTS. A strain lacking that system grows slowly and must compensate. The team measured gene activity across central metabolism in this setting of carbon limitation.

They found changed expression in the genes that burn sugar and run the cell's energy economy. A stress regulator called sigma-38 appears to play a part in keeping those genes active. The picture is a cell rewiring itself around a broken food pipeline. Understanding that rewiring matters for industrial strains built from E. coli. It also shows how bacteria survive scarcity in the wild.
plos-pone-0007566:
Haoquan Wu and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 challenging a tidy assumption about microRNAs. These small RNAs silence genes, and each is cut from a longer precursor by an enzyme called Drosha. The standard view held that Drosha always cuts at the same place. That would give every mature microRNA a fixed start. The team examined the ends of mature microRNAs closely.

The cuts vary more than the textbook picture allows. Alternative processing by Drosha produces mature microRNAs with different 5-prime ends. A shifted start changes which genes the microRNA can target. So this variation is not noise; it widens the silencing repertoire. The finding makes the gene-regulation system look more flexible, and more subtle, than assumed. It also warns researchers to read microRNA sequences with care.
plos-pone-0007666:
Ginny Emerson and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the poxviruses native to North America. Orthopoxviruses include the smallpox virus and its many animal relatives. North America hosts its own endemic set, circulating in wildlife. Their evolutionary relationships and ecology were incompletely charted. The team reconstructed the group's phylogeny, its family tree, and reviewed how the viruses live in nature.

The tree clarifies which North American poxviruses are close kin and which are distant. Ecology explains where each one persists and in which hosts. Such natural history matters for both wildlife health and public health readiness. Poxviruses have surprised the world before. Knowing the local family's structure is basic preparation. The study gives the continent's poxviruses a proper genealogy.
plos-pone-0007766:
Yo-Ping Lai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It clarifies how helper T cells boost killer T cells early in an immune response. Killer CD8 cells attack infected cells, but they do not expand well on their own. Signals plus antigen alone proved insufficient.

The missing help is IL-2, a growth signal made by activated CD4 helper cells. Given during early priming, IL-2 advances the CD8 response. The cells multiply more and gain stronger effector functions. The timing rule matters for vaccine design, where strong killer T cell responses are often the goal.
plos-pone-0007866:
Jacob Lowenstein and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It applies DNA barcoding to a practical problem: naming the tuna in sushi. A short standard DNA stretch can identify a species, like a barcode. The authors tested that idea on tuna sold for sushi, including the prized Thunnus maccoyii.

Seafood is often mislabeled, and tuna species look alike once sliced. Barcodes can expose swaps that cheat buyers and hide overfishing. The authors also contrast barcoding attributes with genetic distances. Their work supports DNA checks as a guard for consumers and for threatened fish stocks.
plos-pone-0007966:
Thomas Vernier and colleagues asked where electric pulses open the cell wall, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pulses that briefly open pores, called electroporation, are a standard way to slip genes or drugs into cells. The team tested whether worn spots in the wall open first.

Their results say yes: fields strike places already harmed by oxidation before sound places. Stressed cells may thus take in more of what the pulse carries than healthy ones do. That bias matters for gene therapy and drug delivery, where the cells most in need may also be the most open.
plos-pone-0008066:
Weiguo Feng and colleagues mapped gene activity as the mouse face forms for PLOS ONE in 2009. The face grows from buds of tissue that swell, meet, and fuse. When fusion fails, cleft lip and palate result, among the most common birth defects.

The team read which genes were active, where, and when, as the buds grew and fused. The atlas shows the order of the building work in fine detail. It also gives a baseline: a gene active at the wrong place or time in this atlas is a prime suspect in facial birth defects.
plos-pone-0008166:
Devon Crawford and colleagues added borrowed temperature channels to rat brain cells and watched for side effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. The channels, TRPV1 and TRPM8, answer to heat and cold. Placed in chosen neurons, they promise remote control of cell firing for research.

Expressing the two channels in hippocampal neurons changed more than temperature response alone. The side effects differed between the two channels, which matters for picking the right tool. A control tool that quietly warps the cells it studies can mislead a whole line of research. The authors report those contrasts channel by channel.
plos-pone-0008266:
Gary Crameri and colleagues created bat cell lines in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Bats are suspected reservoirs for several dangerous emerging viruses. These include Nipah, Hendra, SARS-like coronaviruses, and Ebola. Studying such viruses safely requires bat cells that grow in the lab. Few suitable cell lines existed when the work began.

The team established, immortalised, and characterised lines from pteropid bats. Immortalised lines keep growing instead of dying after a few generations. With them, researchers can test how viruses enter and grow in bat cells. That supports work on preventing the next outbreak.
plos-pone-0008366:
Yun Wang and colleagues studied amyloid effects in rat brains in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Alzheimer's patients show changes in how neurons synchronize their firing. Synchronized network activity supports complex thinking, such as working memory. The mechanisms behind these changes are not understood. Amyloid-beta 42 is a protein fragment central to the disease.

Low and high doses of Aβ42 had opposite effects in the rat prefrontal cortex. Dose flipped the impact on network activity and neuronal excitability. Such a split warns that amount matters in Alzheimer's models. It helps explain conflicting results between studies.
plos-pone-0008466:
Michael Salvatore and co-authors link an enzyme change to movement in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase controls how much dopamine the brain can make. Dopamine is a signal chemical needed for smooth movement. Its precursor, L-DOPA, is a main drug for Parkinson disease. The enzyme's activity shifts when phosphate tags are added. Tags at two sites, ser31 and ser40, play a role.

With aging, the ser31 tag in the nigra gains importance. The nigra is a brain area that loses cells in Parkinson disease. The team tie that tag to how active old animals are. The find helps explain age changes in movement.
plos-pone-0008566:
Laura Musazzi and co-authors test stress effects in rat brains in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Stress is a main risk factor for mental illness. Past work hints that brief stress raises excitatory signals in some brain areas. The team study the front part of the rat cortex. They measure release of glutamate, the main excitatory signal in the brain. Release is triggered by an electric stimulus in the lab tests.

Brief stress raises that glutamate release in the cortex. Drugs used for depression blunt the rise in their tests. A stress-driven surge of glutamate may add to risk of mental illness. Blunting it may be one way those drugs help.
plos-pone-0008666:
Claudine Benard and co-authors study a food additive in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Carrageenan is a high molecular weight sulphated polysaccharide derived from red seaweeds. It is widely used to thicken foods. In rodents, its degraded forms can induce intestinal inflammation, or colitis. That inflammation involves macrophage recruitment and activation. The team analyze how degraded carrageenan acts on monocytes, macrophage precursors in blood.

They find it induces TNF secretion and ICAM-1 upregulation in monocytes through NF-kappaB activation. TNF is a potent inflammatory cytokine. Those effects show a direct path from additive to inflammation in their model. The work informs debate on carrageenan safety in food.
plos-pone-0008766:
Amanda Lorier, Gregory Funk, and John Greer studied how opioids quiet the tongue's nerve supply. Their rat study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tongue muscles keep the airway open during each breath. The hypoglossal nerve drives those muscles. Opioid painkillers depress that nerve and can endanger breathing. A drug class called ampakines boosts nerve signals elsewhere in the brain.

Opiates suppressed hypoglossal motoneuron activity in the rats. Ampakine treatment then restored much of that activity. Reviving tongue drive could protect the airway during opioid use. The result points toward safer pain treatment and overdose care.
plos-pone-0008866:
Veronica Ulici, Claudine James, Katie Hoenselaar, and colleagues listed genes steered by a growth signal in bone-forming cartilage. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Long bones grow at plates of cartilage near their ends. Cartilage cells first multiply, then swell into a mature form. The PI3K signaling pathway influences that sequence. Blocking it earlier had changed growth plate behavior.

The team profiled which genes PI3K controls in growth plate chondrocytes. Lists of responding genes map the pathway's reach in bone growth. Such maps help explain growth disorders of the skeleton. They also guide drugs that touch this common pathway.
plos-pone-0008966:
Khaled Alkhuder and co-authors found a potassium pump that a dangerous bacterium needs to spread, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, also called rabbit fever. It is highly infectious and lives part of its life inside immune cells. Between cells it must survive in body fluids low in potassium.

The team identified a gene, trkH, that builds the bacterium's potassium uptake protein. Mice infected with bacteria lacking trkH saw the germ spread through the body poorly. Without the pump, the bacterium could not thrive outside cells. The pump stands out as a possible weak point for new drugs.
plos-pone-0009066:
Yannis Guillemin and co-authors compared the membrane manners of cell-death proteins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The BCL-2 family includes both killers and protectors of the body's cells. They act by opening or guarding pores in the mitochondrial membrane. How they meet that membrane decides whether a given cell lives or dies.

The team studied active fragments cut from family members of both camps. Pro-death and pro-life fragments behaved distinctly when they met membranes. Each camp's style of approach matched its job inside the cell. The split in membrane behaviour mirrors the family's deep split in function.
plos-pone-0009166:
Enrico Domenici and co-authors screened blood proteins for flags of mental illness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Depression and schizophrenia are still diagnosed by talking about symptoms alone. No blood test backs up the doctor's judgement in the clinic today. Sound biological markers could make diagnosis and treatment checks much firmer.

The team profiled many blood proteins at once in sets of patients and controls. People with depression or schizophrenia were compared with healthy volunteers. Certain proteins in blood plasma set the patient groups measurably apart. Panels of proteins like these are first steps toward lab tests for psychiatry.
plos-pone-0009266:
Lawrence Sirovich, Mark Stoeckle, and Yu Zhang published this biodiversity study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Huge DNA databases now cover life from bacteria to humans. Hidden in those sequences may be a map of how species relate. The authors refined a method that turns DNA sequences into indicator vectors, simple numeric codes.

Plotting those codes reveals the structure of biodiversity in a visual form. Clusters and gaps in the plot reflect real divisions among life forms. The technique needs no family tree built in advance, so it stays open to surprises. It offers a fast way to survey the genetic shape of the living world.
plos-pone-0009366:
Eric Gamazon and co-authors published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gene chips called exon arrays measure how genes are used across the genome. Such data feed studies linking genes to disease and drug response. But DNA variants inside the chip's probes can distort the readings.

The team surveyed the Affymetrix exon array against the 1000 Genomes dataset. They catalogued which probes overlap known SNPs, the single-letter variants people carry. A probe sitting on a variant can fake a change in gene activity. Their catalogue helps researchers clean their data before drawing conclusions.
plos-pone-0011466:
Richard Zhao and co-authors tested in 2010 an unlikely weapon against a stubborn childhood cancer. Neuroblastoma arises from nerve tissue in children, and tumors that resist the drug doxorubicin are nearly untreatable. The team turned to Vpr, a protein made by HIV-1, which is known to stress and kill the cells it enters, and aimed it at the resistant cancer cells.

The viral protein killed doxorubicin-resistant neuroblastoma cells in their tests, succeeding where the standard drug failed. Borrowing a villain's tool is provocative, but the logic is sound: resistance to one killer says nothing about another with a different method. Much work would be needed to deliver such a protein safely and only to tumors. Even so, the study widens the search for resistant-cancer treatments beyond the usual drug families.
plos-pone-0011566:
Ricardo Betancur-R and co-authors combined family trees and body shapes in 2010 to find an invisible border in the sea. A coastal fish of the southern Caribbean split into distinct populations where no ocean barrier, current break, or distance explains the divide. Phylogenetic analysis of its DNA and morphologic analysis of its form agreed on the split, so the team looked to the land for the cause.

They identified a marine biogeographic break of terrestrial origin: a land feature, such as a river's outflow or a past coastline, dividing sea life from the shore side. Geography sculpting ocean diversity from land is a reminder that the two realms share one history. Biogeographic maps drawn only from water will miss such borders. The finding also gives conservation a finer map of Caribbean populations that must be managed as separate stocks.
plos-pone-0011666:
Xiuchun Ge and co-authors developed a faster way to find vaccine targets on a mouth bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus sanguinis normally lives in dental plaque but can also infect the heart. With full genome sequences available, researchers can hunt for surface proteins as vaccine candidates, yet testing them one by one is slow and costly.

Their method immunises with pooled proteins and reads out which surface antigens the immune system recognises. The pooled approach cuts time and animal use while still flagging promising targets. It offers a general shortcut for reverse vaccinology in other bacteria too.
plos-pone-0011766:
Emilie Sapin and co-authors counted brain cells active during excess dream sleep, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Using a staining method that marks recently active neurons, the team had found a massive population in the lower hypothalamus switched on during paradoxical, or REM, sleep hypersomnia. Some of those cells in the tuberal region used the calming transmitter GABA.

Their census shows a very large number of GABAergic neurons are activated there during the hypersomnia state. Mapping this dreaming circuitry in overdrive helps explain how the brain generates and sustains REM sleep, a state tied to memory and mood.
plos-pone-0011866:
Kaushik Ghosal, Andrea Stathopoulos, and Sanjay Pimplikar reported in 2010 on a piece of the Alzheimer's-linked protein APP. APP sits at the center of Alzheimer's research because fragments cut from it form the amyloid found in patients' brains. The team studied a different fragment, the part that stays inside the cell after cutting.

In mice engineered to produce this inner fragment, the birth of new neurons in the adult brain fell, and inflammation in the brain rose alongside. Adult-born neurons support memory, which fades early in Alzheimer's disease. Tying the fragment to inflammation and blocked neuron birth suggests a route of harm quite separate from the plaques that get most attention.
plos-pone-0011966:
Vivien Béziat and co-workers charted in 2010 the final maturation steps of natural killer cells, a front-line immune cell type. Mature NK cells must stay broadly ready for trouble while sparing healthy tissue, a balance taught during their education. Two receptor families, KIRs and NKG2A, carry much of that teaching.

Tracking both across development showed a stepwise pattern: NKG2A levels fall in a coordinated way as KIRs are acquired. That ordered handover gives immunologists a ruler for judging how mature a patient's NK cells are. It also sharpens thinking about NK cell therapies, where the maturation state of infused cells may decide how well they work.
plos-pone-0012066:
Sarrah Castillo and co-workers made in 2010 a first list of the immune gene forms found in raccoons, the chief land carrier of rabies in North America. The genes belong to the MHC set, which shows bits of germs to the immune system so it can learn them. The set's wide range of forms is kept up in part by germ pressure. Most wild-life work on these genes had passed this species by.

The team read two key parts of the raccoon's MHC genes and set down the forms they found. A base list of immune range in the top rabies host helps work on how rabies lasts and spreads in the wild. It also bears on why the bait vaccines dropped for raccoons work well in some places and poorly in others.
plos-pone-0012166:
Guillaume Dumas, Jacqueline Nadel, Robert Soussignan, and co-authors studied two brains working at once during social interaction, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When two people interact, each keeps adjusting to the other in real time, and a shared rhythm often emerges from that back-and-forth. Most brain studies look at one person alone, which misses the coupling that makes interaction what it is.

Recording both partners at once, the team found their brain activity can synchronize during the exchange. That coupling is a physical trace of mutual adaptation between people. It opens a way to study social difficulties, such as those in autism, as problems of coordination between brains rather than faults inside one brain alone.
plos-pone-0012266:
Smriti Mehra, Bapi Pahar, Noton Dutta, and co-authors read gene activity inside tuberculosis granulomas in monkeys, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A granuloma is the dense ball of cells the body builds to wall off tuberculosis bacteria in the lung. The wall should contain the infection, yet the bacteria have evolved ways to live inside it, sometimes for decades.

Profiling which host genes switch on or off inside these structures shows how the standoff is maintained, and where the bacteria gain the upper hand. Monkeys mirror human tuberculosis closely, so their granulomas speak to human disease. That knowledge guides vaccines and drugs meant to tip the balance toward the host.
plos-pone-0012366:
Thomas Riess, Maryline Achieng, Samuel Otieno and co-workers interviewed circumcised men in Kisumu, Kenya, for a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Trials had shown that circumcision cuts a man's risk of catching HIV through sex by more than half. Health experts worried that newly circumcised men might feel fully safe and take more risks, wiping out the gain.

Through interviews, the men described what they were taught during the rite and how their behavior changed after. Some did report riskier behavior, tied in part to beliefs about what circumcision protects against. The findings tell HIV programs to pair circumcision with strong counseling, so men keep using other protection as well.
plos-pone-0012466:
William Weldon, Bao-Zhong Wang, Maria Martin and colleagues strengthened a flu vaccine protein, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The swine-origin H1N1 pandemic showed how slowly egg-grown vaccines arrive. One faster route builds vaccines from the flu surface protein hemagglutinin alone, but the lone protein is a weak immune trigger, especially when it falls apart.

The team stabilized the protein in its three-part trimer form, the shape the immune system meets on real virus. The stabilized version provoked stronger immunity in their tests. Sturdier vaccine proteins could mean faster, egg-free flu vaccines when the next pandemic strain appears.
plos-pone-0012566:
Renee Ruhaak, Hae-Won Uh, Marian Beekman and colleagues hunted blood markers of healthy human aging, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Markers that reflect true health in old age, not just years lived, are extremely scarce yet valuable. Antibodies wear sugar coats whose patterns shift with age and disease, so the team read the sugar forms on IgG antibodies.

One form — IgG carrying a bisecting GlcNAc sugar — was notably lower in long-lived people. A sugar signature tied to longevity could help researchers measure whether lifestyle or drugs truly slow aging. It also links immune aging to the broader biology of the long-lived.
plos-pone-0012666:
Saisongkorh, Robert, La Scola and co-authors found gene swapping between bacteria that live inside amoebae. Bartonella bacteria live inside mammal blood cells, a tight and sheltered home. Computer scans of their genomes hinted that they still trade genes with other bacteria despite that shelter.

Their 2010 work gives evidence that type IV secretion genes passed between Bartonella and Rhizobium radiobacter inside amoebae. Shared amoeba homes may act as mixing vessels for bacterial genes. Such swaps can hand pathogens new tools, so tracking them matters for disease science and for watching how new traits spread.
plos-pone-0012766:
Gossens, Naus, Hollander and co-authors found that mice missing the protein ADAM8 grow an overfull thymus. The thymus trains T cells, and its work needs constant traffic between young T cells and the tissue around them. Proteases that trim the matrix and free signals help that traffic flow.

Their 2010 knockout mice ended up with far more thymus cells than normal. That surplus suggests ADAM8 normally reins in T cell growth or movement there. The result informs how the immune system's schoolhouse is kept in balance.  Cell counts made the difference large and easy to measure.
pmc-2815666:
Kabsch explains the working principles behind key steps in processing X-ray rotation data, as carried out by his program XDS. Rotation data come from turning a crystal in an X-ray beam and recording diffraction images as it moves. Each image must be merged into one consistent dataset.

The paper walks through integration, scaling, space-group assignment, and post-refinement: turning spots on images into measured intensities, correcting differences between images, and fixing the crystal's symmetry. Clear accounts of these steps help crystallographers judge data quality before building atomic models.  Post-refinement then polishes the merged data before structure solution begins in earnest.
pmc-3552766:
Tong, Flemming, McInnes, and co-authors develop ENTREQ, guidance for reporting syntheses of qualitative research. Combining findings across qualitative studies can reveal patterns across contexts, build new models, and expose research gaps. Such syntheses also inform the development and evaluation of health interventions.

Without transparent reporting, readers cannot judge how a synthesis was done. ENTREQ lists what authors should disclose about searching, appraising, and combining studies. The statement raised standards in a growing field, helping decision makers use patients' experiences with the same rigour as trial data.  Review teams in nursing and psychology adapted the checklist for their fields.
pmc-4174766:
Kawasaki and Kawai reviewed Toll-like receptor signaling in 2014. Toll-like receptors, or TLRs, are key sensors of the innate immune system, the body's first line of defense. They detect patterns that are typical of microbes and not found in human cells.

Once a receptor spots such a pattern, it recruits adaptor molecules inside the cell. That chain switches on transcription factors, including one known as NF-kappaB, which turn on defense genes. The review maps these pathways step by step for each receptor type. Knowing the routes helps explain infections and inflammation, and guides drugs that tune the immune response.
pmc-4283466:
Sheldrick presented SHELXT in 2015, a computer program for solving crystal structures. Crystallographers measure reflections from a single crystal and must solve the phase problem to recover the structure. SHELXT uses a new dual-space algorithm to do this, working from data expanded into a simple space group.

The program takes missing data into account and extends resolution when needed. It also works out the true space group as part of the same run. That integration saves steps that once took separate programs and expert judgment. SHELXT became a first tool many labs run when a new crystal yields fresh diffraction data.
pmc-7190266:
Mhairi Campbell, Joanne McKenzie, Amanda Sowden, and coauthors wrote the SWiM reporting guideline in 2020. Some systematic reviews cannot pool results in a meta-analysis. Authors then synthesize findings in words or tables, often with little method detail.

SWiM, short for synthesis without meta-analysis, sets nine items such reviews should report. They cover how studies were grouped, how effects were compared, and how certainty was judged. Clearer reporting lets readers check whether the summary is fair. Journals began asking authors to follow the guideline soon after it appeared. A checklist version of the guideline is provided for authors and journal editors.
pmc-8476166:
Mosè Manni and co-authors updated BUSCO in 2021, a widely used method for scoring how complete a genome assembly is. BUSCO judges data by looking for genes expected to appear exactly once in nearly every species of a group. Finding most of them suggests a complete assembly, while duplicates hint at errors or contamination.

The update adds streamlined workflows and extends coverage across eukaryotes, prokaryotes, and viruses, so more kinds of data can be scored the same way. The authors describe the new gene sets and how the scoring runs. Because nearly every genome project reports a BUSCO score, changes to this tool ripple through the whole field's quality standards.
plos-pone-0345766:
Song Fang and colleagues developed in 2026 a model for judging driving risk inside urban road tunnels. Tunnels concentrate several hazards at once: sudden changes in light at the entrances, narrow lanes with walls close by, and no room to escape a crash. A risk model gives engineers and tunnel operators a structured way to score how dangerous a tunnel or a driving situation is.

The authors build their model around the factors that drive tunnel accidents, so that risk can be assessed before crashes supply the data the hard way. Cities keep adding road tunnels as they grow, and traffic through them is heavy. A sound risk model supports decisions on speed limits, lighting, ventilation, and emergency planning.
plos-pone-0360066:
Peiyuan Liu, Tania Espinosa, Elham Samami, Bernard Mensah, and Hermine Poghosyan wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It studies adults in ten United States states and the link between economic instability and substance use. The work is population-based, drawing on a broad sample rather than a clinic group.

Economic instability covers insecure work, income swings, and trouble meeting basic costs. Tying that instability to substance use helps explain why addiction clusters where livelihoods are shaky. Public health officials designing prevention programs can use state-level evidence to argue for pairing treatment with economic support services.
plos-pone-0359866:
Cartrine Anyango, Isabel Goicolea, and Fredinah Namatovu published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Set in Sweden, it assesses whether formal service providers are ready to address intimate partner violence among women with disabilities. The analysis uses mixed methods, combining surveys with deeper qualitative material.

Women with disabilities face high rates of partner violence and extra barriers when seeking help. Readiness covers whether police, health, and social services can recognize abuse and respond accessibly. Swedish service planners, and disability advocates pressing for safer services, are the readers for this readiness check.
plos-pone-0359566:
Yingzhe Wang and six colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on a medicinal plant, Eupatorium lindleyanum. Using multi-omics integration, several layers of molecular data combined, the authors reveal how sesquiterpenoids are made. These plant chemicals, thought to carry much of the plant's healing value, are made differently in different tissues.

Knowing which tissue makes which compound tells growers and chemists which plant parts to harvest and when. Tissue-specific production also hints at the genes worth breeding or engineering for stronger medicine. Researchers of healing plants and natural drug chemistry are the audience for this molecular map.
plos-pone-0357566: Vásquez-Arévalo and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on birds, fruit, and forest regrowth in southern Brazil. They mapped which birds eat fruit from which plants in two young Araucaria forests. These feeding webs show how seeds get carried to new ground. When key birds vanish, tree spread can stall. The maps help managers plan how to help damaged forests heal.
plos-pone-0359266: Landa and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE case study on water, sanitation, and hygiene guidance in Indonesia. The guidance aims to be climate-resilient and inclusive, so services hold up under floods and reach everyone. The team used mixed methods to study how the guidance was put into practice. Lessons from one country can help others adapt similar guidance to local risks.
plos-pone-0358866: Yang and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on software that finds flaws on steel surfaces. Their network, EMamba, adds a mixture-of-experts design to a state space model. The goal is sturdy detection even when lighting or steel type changes. Missed cracks in steel can fail later in bridges or machines, so reliable automated inspection has real safety value.
plos-pone-0359066:
Ahmad Bishr Nasra leads a team of eight surveying whether patients in Syria care about their doctor's sex, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. In conservative settings, comfort with a male or female physician can shape whether people seek care at all, especially for private examinations. Local evidence was thin, so the team questioned adults at major public teaching hospitals across several centers.

For everyday matters and most routine interactions, many respondents said they had no preference. The picture changed for intimate examinations, where patients strongly favored a doctor of their own sex. Women leaned toward female doctors for intimate and reproductive care, while men more often chose male doctors even for general examinations. The findings help hospitals think about staffing and scheduling where patient comfort decides attendance.
europmc-pmc7067566: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at variable forecasting accuracy of polygenic scores within an ancestry group. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. A sharper test or warning sign can change outcomes, since earlier care usually works better.
gao-gaoreports-b-311266: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at Gloria Kortum. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions. The full text sits with this description in the library.
europmc-pmc8444066: A fresh look at perturbations in gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) composition in psychiatric illnesses: a review arrived with this 2021 research paper. Importance evidence of gut microbiota (the microbes living in the body) perturbations has accumulated for multiple psychiatric illnesses. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-366: The Government Accountability Office dug into chemical and Biological Defense: DOD and VA Need to Improve Efforts to Identify and Notify Individuals Potentially Exposed during Chemical and Biological Tests in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
europmc-pmc8013866: Ishida and co-authors published this research paper in 2021 on E3 ligase ligands for protacs: how they were found and how to discover new ones. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc8092566: A 2021 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at learning loss due to school closures during. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7182166: Pal and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on severe acute breathing syndrome Coronavirus-2: an update. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
europmc-pmc7734766: Kawel-Boehm and co-authors published this research paper in 2020 on reference ranges ("normal values") for cardiovascular (of the heart and blood vessels) magnetic resonance in adults and children: 2020 update. The team describes what it did and what it found, step by step. Findings like these get picked up, tested, and built on by other teams.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-466: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands: Pending Legislation Would Apply US Immigration Law to the CNMI with a Transition Period. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-566: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on value-Added Taxes: Lessons Learned from Other Countries on Compliance Risks, Administrative Costs, Compliance Burden, and Transition. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-966: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on rebuilding Iraq: DOD and State Department Have Improved Oversight and Coordination of Private Security Contractors in Iraq, but Further Actions Are Needed to Su. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
europmc-pmc7870666: Published in 2021, this research paper takes on characterization (detailed description) of ferroptosis (an iron-driven form of cell death) in kidney tubular cell death under diabetic (of diabetes) conditions. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-866: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at DOD Business Transformation: Air Force's Current Approach Increases Risk That Asset Visibility Goals and Transformation Priorities Will Not Be Achieved. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
europmc-pmc7190266: A 2020 research paper from the Europe PMC archive looks at synthesis without meta-analysis (a study pooling many studies) in systematic (thorough) reviews: reporting guideline. It combines data from many other studies to reach a firmer answer. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc7215166: A fresh look at preventing problematic internet use during the COVID-19 pandemic: shared view guidance arrived with this 2020 research paper. As a reply to the COVID-19 pandemic, many governments have introduced steps such as spatial distancing and "staying at home". Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc8184766: This 2021 research paper covers b cell signatures and tertiary lymphoid structures contribute to outcome (result) in head and neck squamous cell. The current immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system) paradigms aim to reinvigorate CD8 + t cells, but the contribution. plos-pone-0358966:
Solomon Daniel Halilu leads a team of seven asking Nigerian medical students how they want to be taught, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The survey covered one hundred seventy-one students at Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University in Bauchi and mixed counted answers with written comments. Lectures, problem based learning, team learning, practical demonstrations, and digital tools were all on the table.

Practical demonstrations won, chosen by about a third, followed by small group activities at about a quarter. The biggest complaint was trouble retaining information, named by nearly half, with a smaller share feeling underprepared for clinical work. Students asked for teaching tied closely to real patients, lecturers who know their subjects deeply, and consultants who also mentor. The authors recommend more hands on and group learning, better clinical exposure, and stronger digital facilities in the curriculum.
plos-pone-0358066:
Joseph Mwaka, Conrad Sserunjogi, and Jesca Natalayi catalogue the tumours found in patients at a specialized HIV centre in Kampala, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They reviewed two hundred nineteen tumour records at Mildmay Hospital, spanning 2017 into 2026. For each growth they noted whether it was malignant. They also recorded the patient's immune status and virus control at diagnosis, in the modern era of effective HIV treatment.

Nearly two thirds of the tumours were malignant, and Kaposi sarcoma alone supplied almost half of the cancers. Most patients had their virus suppressed at diagnosis, yet over half of those suppressed cases were still malignant. Cancer clustered in patients who had started treatment late: low immune cell counts, advanced disease stage, and fewer months on therapy before the tumour appeared. The authors caution these are unadjusted patterns, but they set a baseline for a planned prospective cancer cohort at the centre.
plos-pone-0358566:
Hala Alkhoury leads a team of six assembling the first large picture of gunshot wounds treated across the Palestinian West Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Eight hospitals contributed records for three hundred ninety-two patients treated between 2020 and 2025. Nearly all were male, and the typical patient was a teenager or young man of about nineteen. The study maps where bullets struck, what surgery was needed, and how patients fared.

Limbs took most injuries, about two thirds, and broken bones were the commonest accompanying damage. Chest, belly, and blood vessel wounds were rarer but far more dangerous. Over half the patients needed surgery, most often bone fixation or vessel repair. One in five required intensive care, about three percent died in hospital, and more than half of survivors left with some dependence on others. A fast pulse and abdominal injury best predicted intensive care need.
plos-pone-0358366:
Hui Zeng leads a team of seven mapping the uncertainty that shadows women treated for gynecologic and breast cancers, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Not knowing what comes next corrodes mental health, especially where support is thin. Four hundred thirteen patients at a Beijing hospital completed scales for uncertainty, support, depression, and anxiety. Statistical profiling sorted the women by how uncertainty presented, and a structural model tested whether uncertainty links support to depression.

Three profiles emerged. A small group, about eight percent, combined low uncertainty with good adaptation. The largest, over half, lived with high uncertainty and a foggy grasp of their disease. Education, who provided care, time since diagnosis, support, and depression all separated the groups. The modeling placed uncertainty in the middle of the support to depression pathway. Screening for the fog itself could catch struggling patients that symptom checklists miss.
plos-pone-0357466:
José Luís Pimenta, João Carlos Paiva, and Maria João Fonseca published a museum education study from Portugal in PLOS ONE in 2026. They asked children in a program called Young Naturalists what they think of natural history museums. Adult planners often guess at what holds a child's interest; this team asked the children directly.

Pimenta and his colleagues gathered the children's own views on what draws them in and what leaves them cold. Answers like these help museum staff design visits that spark real curiosity instead of passive walking. For any museum trying to serve young visitors, the study is a reminder to build programs with children's voices in the room.
plos-pone-0356366:
Farai Nyabadza modeled a dark side of prisons in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Jailing people for petty crimes may increase later crime, if prison exposes minor offenders to harder criminal influence. Nyabadza built a model to quantify that criminogenic effect, the degree to which incarceration itself breeds crime.

The model's numbers put a measurable size on the school-of-crime effect that reformers have long warned about. Policymakers weighing short sentences for minor offenses gain a cost rarely shown in budgets: future victims and future prison load. Even readers who favor tough sentencing benefit from seeing the trade-off priced. Sentencing debates improve when both sides must answer the same arithmetic.
plos-pone-0346466:
Varsha Bommineni led a team of five authors mapping gene activity in chickens with spotty liver disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease cuts egg production and costs the industry heavily. The team read the full set of active genes in the liver, the organ at the center of the illness.

Bommineni's gene-level picture shows how birds respond as the disease attacks, which defenses switch on and which pathways fail. That map points to where vaccines or breeding could help most. Poultry diseases spread fast in dense flocks, so molecular insight that arrives before an outbreak is worth far more than insight after. The study gives the egg industry a molecular baseline for this costly disease.
plos-pone-0358266:
Panthip Patrakunwiwat led a team of eight authors comparing two lifelines for newborn hearts, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Some babies are born with lung circulation that depends on a fetal vessel staying open. Doctors can keep flow with a stent in that vessel, or with a surgical shunt called a modified Blalock-Taussig shunt.

Patrakunwiwat's team compared how the lung arteries change after each approach. That growth matters because these babies later need full repair surgery, and vessel size shapes its success. Head-to-head results guide heart teams choosing the safer bridge for each fragile newborn. Both options save lives; the question is which grows better arteries with fewer problems.
plos-pone-0358466:
Ya-Ling Hsieh, Chia-Jung Chiang, and Tsung Yu published a 2026 population study in PLOS ONE on childbirth after cancer among women in Taiwan. As survival improves, more women diagnosed during their reproductive years wonder whether they can still have children, but Asian population data were scarce. The authors linked Taiwan's cancer, birth, and death registries to follow tens of thousands of women diagnosed at age thirty-nine or younger.

About one survivor in ten had a live birth after diagnosis, and overall survivors had roughly half the births expected in the general population. Outcomes differed sharply by cancer type: thyroid and skin cancer survivors kept childbearing nearly intact, while cervical, uterine, breast, blood, and brain cancers cut it most. Older age at diagnosis and chemotherapy also lowered the chances. The authors press for early fertility counseling and better access to fertility-preserving care.
plos-pone-0357966:
Shuting Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 gene study in PLOS ONE on how the heart adapts when oxygen stays low for a long time. Chronic low oxygen is a driver of cardiovascular disease, but its effects on heart tissue were tangled up with two other patterns: low oxygen before birth, and a shorter adult exposure. Using three public gene-expression datasets, the team compared the patterns side by side, with extensive permutation testing.

Each pattern produced its own distinct set of changed genes, with no overlap between the groups. The sustained pattern rewired the heart's daily clock network heavily: links between clock genes thinned by about two-thirds, while one gene, ASS1, became a central hub. Changed genes split into two camps, metabolic-immune versus clock pathways, with matching splits in linked diseases and drug targets. Long-term oxygen shortage, they say, reshapes heart biology along two separate tracks.
plos-pone-0356266:
Hanye Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 plant pathology paper in PLOS ONE on detecting a damaging passionfruit virus, East Asian Passiflora virus, with a new laboratory test. The virus spreads through China's passionfruit regions and cuts yields, so growers need fast, certain diagnosis. The team built a real-time fluorescence test targeting the virus's coat protein gene and tuned it carefully.

The assay proved highly specific, flagging only the target virus, and roughly a thousand times more sensitive than the older standard test, detecting very small amounts of viral material. It found the virus in deliberately infected plants and in leaves the infection reached on its own. In 2025, one hundred twenty suspect samples from Yunnan Province all tested positive, confirming how established the virus is there. The assay is offered as a surveillance tool for nurseries and regional monitoring programs.
plos-pone-0357666:
Yuta Nemoto and co-authors ran a small pilot trial in Yokosuka, Japan, asking whether video game contests can help older adults stay sharp and active. Their 2026 program mixed health lessons, exercise, and organized gaming in weekly sessions over about three months. Adults aged sixty and over who had never played digital games took part, split between the program group and a comparison group.

No one was harmed, nearly everyone stayed, and all players said they enjoyed the sessions. Mood scores rose after each meeting, and walking speed and balance improved more in the gaming group than in the comparison group. Nemoto and colleagues stress that the trial was small and exploratory, so larger studies must confirm any real benefit.
plos-pone-0356566:
Takuya Nishioka and colleagues tested a shortcut for profiling leg strength. Instead of pressing against many loads, use just two, one light and one heavy. The loads chart how force falls as speed rises. Their 2026 study had sixteen young men perform maximal leg presses on a pneumatic machine. Eleven loads were used. Full profiles were then compared against profiles computed from ten possible load pairs.

Pairs spanning a wide gap reproduced the full profile almost perfectly. The lightest load worked best against loads at roughly two and a half to three times body weight. Pairs with close-together loads degraded quickly. Coaches use these profiles to target training. A valid two-load test saves athletes a long, exhausting testing session, provided the two loads are chosen far apart.
plos-pone-0355466:
Corinna Urmann and colleagues tackled a classic trap in hunting antiviral compounds in plants. One common chlorophyll breakdown product, pheophorbide A, blocks viruses so reliably that it drowns out every subtler candidate in a screening test. Their 2026 study built a leveling strategy. It measured each extract's pheophorbide content. It judged the extract's antiviral effect against what that content alone predicts.

Six of fifteen plant species cleared the bar and earned priority for deeper work. In cowslip fractions, the comparison plus chemical profiling pointed to additional candidate molecules beyond the usual suspect. The method generalizes. Any natural product screen haunted by one dominant compound can use the same accounting trick to find the quieter chemistry hiding behind it.
plos-pone-0356766:
Un-Kon Lee reviewed five years of worldwide AI ethics principles. They came from governments, think tanks, and technology companies. His goal was to update South Korea's national set. His 2026 study combined thirty-seven prior reviews into seventeen candidate principles. It ranked their standing across the field. It tracked how rankings shifted around 2020, when most national sets appeared.

Three principles proved durable everywhere: transparency, robustness, and a ban on rights infringement. Five others rose or lagged in use and need fresh emphasis. They include responsibility, well-being, human rights, controllability, and sustainability. Lee proposes expanding Korea's ten principles to fourteen. His analysis also flags which ideals are both valued and well served, and which need governing machinery built urgently.
plos-pone-0354366:
Shabnam Varmazyari and three colleagues compare how Iranian dentists and their patients feel about dentists counseling smokers to quit, in this 2026 two-phase survey. Dentists see smokers' mouths regularly, making the dental chair an underused front against tobacco. The study canvassed all dentists in Tehran province's comprehensive health centers and several hundred patients at city centers, a few years apart, asking about attitudes and what shapes them.

Non-smoking dentists held notably more positive attitudes toward offering cessation counseling, as did those working in the city itself. Among patients, non-smokers were more likely to judge such counseling effective, while patients with a smoker in the family were less convinced. Employed patients found oral symptoms a stronger motive to quit and were more willing to try quitting with dental support. The authors suggest mentoring for smoking dentists, remote training for rural ones, and workplace-based programs.
plos-pone-0355866:
Md Mahfuz Islam, Richard McLaughlin, and Joshua Heitman test whether mixing compost into construction-battered soil can help cities absorb stormwater, in this 2026 laboratory study. Building work compacts soil until rain runs off instead of soaking in.
