The team packed soil columns with two soil types and two compost recipes at four mixing rates, then ran water through them repeatedly over six months while tracking the soil's physical condition.

At the two higher rates, the soil grew lighter and more porous and held more plant-available water. Infiltration was fastest at the highest compost rate, roughly ten times the untreated soil, with middle rates close behind; gains steadied after about two months but lasted the full trial. Compost type made no difference. The authors suggest at least a thirty percent mix is needed for a real stormwater benefit.
plos-pone-0354966:
Luca Martino and co-authors propose a way to show uncertainty when choosing how complex a statistical model should be. Analysts often must pick a number of components, or how strongly to shrink a model toward simplicity. Their 2026 paper gives two procedures that return a plausible range instead of a single guessed value.

Both procedures read the shape of the error curve, so they need no probability model for the data. Tests on made-up and real datasets showed the ranges worked well in practice. The methods apply across regression, classification, clustering, and related tasks. Martino and colleagues also share MATLAB code, so other researchers can use the approach directly.
plos-pone-0347366:
Ihor Kendiukhov stress-tested a habit in gene science: trust that mouse gene wiring holds in humans. Labs match genes by descent and borrow the wiring, but no one had checked how often the loan pays off. The 2026 study built gene links from human and mouse lung cells apart, then set them side by side.

Links matched well when the organ was the same, far past chance. The sign of each link, boost or brake, matched for all the strongest ones. But the match was patchy. Links for cell-identity genes, which mark what a cell is, crossed species near intact. Links for signal genes barely crossed at all. Borrowed wiring is safe for identity, shaky for signals.
plos-pone-0355166:
Alaa Abdulelah Alansari and co-authors gauged smoke exposure in Saudi women with a urine test, not just with self-reports. Shame makes many women hide smoking, so surveys miss the truth. Their 2026 study took urine from one hundred thirty-three women who also filled forms on smoking and on smoke breathed from others.

The team proved out a fine lab method for cotinine, the stuff nicotine breaks down into, which stays in urine. The method was true and tight across the range they need. They set cut points fit for this group to split smokers from non-smokers. Alansari and colleagues say body tests should back up surveys where shame skews frank replies.
plos-pone-0356066:
Rebecca Dudovitz and co-authors compared how families report adverse childhood experiences in clinic versus by telephone. Screening for childhood adversity can trigger help, but only if parents answer fully and honestly. Their 2026 study re-screened, by a community helpline's telephone service, families who had already completed the same screen at well-child visits.

Fifty-one families from three community health centres took part in the within-family comparison. The analysis asked whether scores shifted between settings and which family traits, including trust in healthcare, predicted any shift. Dudovitz and colleagues frame screening mode as a design choice with consequences: the same questions may harvest different truths depending on who asks, and where.
plos-pone-0354466:
Ruoyan Pei and colleagues present in 2026 a two stage detection system for finding road users in poor light, blending normal camera and heat images. Distant small objects give weak signals, and glare or darkness degrades each image type in its own way. The first stage fuses the two views with gated attention, and the second links candidate objects in a graph to reason about their layout.

Tests on two public datasets showed much stronger results across day and night, with the day to night gap shrinking dramatically. Small object detection improved a lot, and speed stayed fast enough for real time use. Self driving systems in hard conditions could benefit.
plos-pone-0353666:
Ji Eun Song, Mi Yeon Lee, Chungkwon Yoo, and Joon Mo Kim published this 2026 study of eye pressure and women's reproductive history in South Korea. Using a national health survey, they analyzed more than eighteen hundred women past menopause. They related age at first period, age at menopause, and reproductive span to pressure inside the eye, split by whether the women had glaucoma.

Longer estrogen exposure tracked with higher eye pressure in women without glaucoma, but with lower pressure in women with glaucoma. Song calls estrogen's role context dependent, with possible use in judging glaucoma risk.
plos-pone-0344266:
Quanlong Fan, Gang Xu, Yunge Wang, and Mengke Wu published this 2026 computer science paper on spotting real-world events in social media streams. Posts mix text, images, and video, and older detectors usually read only one source. Their framework links posts into a graph and uses graph neural networks with cross-modal attention to weigh words and pictures together.

Checked against news coverage from the same period, adding images and news to text improved how accurately events were found and classified. Fan offers the design for faster, fuller awareness during fast-moving public events.
plos-pone-0353166:
La and colleagues, writing in 2026, introduce a new language resource for Vietnamese government work. Their team built a large set of labeled administrative texts, meant to teach computers to find named items in official papers. Older Vietnamese data sets drew mostly on news or health texts, which left a gap for formal state documents.

The new corpus holds a very large number of sentences marked for five kinds of items, such as agencies, legal papers, dates, and amounts. Human checkers agreed closely on the labels, which supports trust in the data. The authors also test a model that pairs a Vietnamese language model with a step that keeps labels in a sensible order. That model beat older methods on their tests, and the data set is shared in public for other teams to use.
plos-pone-0354666: Pregnant women in Garowe, Somalia — anemia and its factors. This antenatal care study documented them. The findings give Puntland’s health system the risk factors to target — because anemic mothers bear vulnerable babies.
plos-pone-0353266:
La and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask American health professionals what they know and do about RSV, a respiratory virus that can hospitalize older adults. Vaccines for adults are new, uptake is low, and doctors' own gaps may be part of the problem. Seven hundred clinicians, from primary care doctors to pharmacists, answered during the 2024-25 season.

Most said they were very familiar with the disease, yet real gaps showed on who the vaccines are approved for and what national advisers recommend. The most common barriers were patients refusing or hesitating, and patients simply never having heard of RSV. Only about a third of workplaces stocked the vaccine, though most clinicians said they recommend it to eligible patients. Recommendations, however, were not made consistently to everyone eligible. The authors point to education for clinicians and patients alike as the fastest lever.
plos-pone-0327266:
John Baptist Asiimwe and five colleagues measure how widespread chronic diseases are among Kenyan men, in this 2026 PLOS ONE analysis of a national health survey. The data cover more than fourteen thousand men aged fifteen to fifty-four, interviewed in 2022. The diseases counted include high blood pressure, diabetes, heart and lung disease, arthritis, depression, anxiety, and cancer.

About one man in eleven reported at least one such condition, and roughly one in fifty lived with several at once. High blood pressure was the most common, followed by depression. Risk rose with age, wealth, region, and sedentary habits. The authors argue men's health checks in Kenya should look beyond infections to these slower, lasting illnesses.
plos-pone-0354266:
Xiang Feng and six colleagues piece together the molecular structure of a particular Chinese coal, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Knowing coal's exact structure helps engineers burn and convert it more cleanly. Their sample was a high-volatile bituminous coal from Inner Mongolia. Four laboratory techniques probed its elements, carbon skeleton, chemical groups, and nitrogen forms from different angles.

Combining the readings, they proposed a single large molecule with a stated formula, built from small aromatic rings linked by carbon and oxygen chains. Its oxygen sits mainly in phenol and ether groups, its nitrogen in ring structures. Simulated spectra matched the real measurements, supporting the model as a working picture of this coal.
plos-pone-0353866:
Andras Dobos and seven colleagues test a hormone-like drug against eye inflammation in mice, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The drug, maxadilan, activates a receptor that calms inflammation and swelling, and the team wanted to know whether it could protect the cornea. Mice were given a bacterial toxin that triggers eye inflammation, followed by the drug injected into the eye.

Scans showed less corneal swelling and better-preserved tissue in treated animals. Eye pressure dropped, fewer inflammatory cells gathered in the eye fluid, and several inflammatory signals fell. Microscope checks confirmed the cornea kept its normal structure. The authors propose this receptor as a promising target for treating inflamed eyes.
plos-pone-0353766:
David Madden analyses how countries' COVID-19 death tolls compare once their different age structures are handled fairly, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Older populations naturally suffer more in a pandemic, so crude comparisons mislead. Using a standard dataset of short-term mortality, Madden recalculated excess deaths with one shared age distribution, and also counted years of life lost, then related the results to national income and inequality.

The recalculations moved individual countries somewhat but barely shuffled the overall ranking. Richer countries generally fared better; inequality showed no clear link. Former planned economies of central and eastern Europe clustered together with poor outcomes. Rankings, he concludes, are sturdier than critics of excess-death statistics suggest.
plos-pone-0353966:
Marcelo Bueno and eight colleagues ask whether a field's cropping history helps predict how much carbon its soil holds, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of Peru's northern highlands. Andean soils are carbon-rich but threatened as farming expands. The team trained a satellite-based classifier on more than five hundred fields to reconstruct which crops rotated where between 2019 and 2022, then tested whether that history improved a soil-carbon model.

The full model explained about two thirds of the variation. Soil properties themselves mattered most, but among management signals, how often a field lay fallow was the strongest single clue. Dropping climate data hurt the model more than dropping rotation history — useful guidance for where to spend measurement effort.
plos-pone-0352966:
Rana Ali Al-Qaari and seven colleagues build a questionnaire on folic acid. It had to work across two very different cultures. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. Folic acid before pregnancy prevents serious birth defects. Yet awareness varies widely. Five hundred and thirty-eight women completed the new tool. They lived in Thailand and Yemen. The tool has eight knowledge questions and ten attitude questions. Experts helped develop it. It was tested twice for stability.

The attitude section performed strongly in both countries. Its structure held together well. Knowledge was patchier. Women knew food sources and timing best. They knew the underlying biology least. The Yemeni knowledge section held together less tightly. A shared tool lets health programmes compare barriers honestly across borders.
plos-pone-0352166:
Singh and colleagues designed a gene edit for rohu, a major food fish, in a 2026 study. The target was a gene that slows muscle growth, so switching it off could one day yield bigger fish for farming. All of the work was done by design and computer checks, before any live fish would be changed.

The team built a short piece of donor DNA with one letter swapped to create an early stop signal in the gene. Lab checks confirmed the swap was in place, and computer models predicted the gene product would be cut short and lose its normal shape. Readers get a tested blueprint for a future breeding step, not a finished fish.
plos-pone-0353466:
Muhammad Danyal and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One paper on teaching computers to write captions that describe what is happening in a picture. Many automatic caption systems match words without grasping how objects relate to each other, so their captions come out thin. The team combined an object-detection model with a text-generating transformer that also encodes where objects sit in the image.

Against two older approaches, the new system scored best on measures that reward meaning and object relationships, even though it trailed on one word-matching score. Human experts also rated its captions highly for accuracy across several hundred test images. The work points toward image descriptions that are more useful for search, accessibility, and content sorting.
plos-pone-0350166:
Tom Moorhouse and five colleagues investigate this 2026 PLOS One study of conflict between people and elephants in villages along the edge of South Africa's Kruger National Park. Elephants that leave the park can endanger residents and crops, and some are killed under current policy. The team combined community surveys with social media accounts of one incident in the village of Matsulu, where an elephant died.

Both sources pointed the same way: some residents tampered with the park fence and lured elephants out, gaining meat and, for a few, money, while the wider community bore the costs. Most survey respondents still backed non-lethal ways of managing elephants. The authors recommend re-examining the policy that allows escaped elephants to be killed, since it may reward the very escapes it aims to handle.
plos-pone-0341766:
John Rong Hao Tay and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One paper on the creation of a large oral disease registry at Singapore's national dental center. The registry pulls together electronic health records to standardize information on dental and mouth diseases across the country's largest healthcare group. The authors explain how it was governed and built, and profile the patients recorded between 2013 and mid-2025.

The registry now holds records for well over two hundred thousand patients, roughly half women and half men, with an average age near fifty. Those records reveal a heavy burden of tooth loss and gum disease, including many advanced periodontitis cases. As Singapore's first resource of this scale for oral health, it gives researchers and planners real-world data for improving dental services.
plos-pone-0352866:
Robert Davis and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS One primer explaining the daily temperature swing, the gap between a day's high and low, for health researchers. Large swings are often linked to illness and death, but the weather behind them is rarely explained. Using a detailed climate archive, the team mapped how the swing has changed across the mainland United States from 1950 through 2022.

The daily swing has shrunk over most of the country, because nights are warming faster than days as air grows more humid and cloudy. The most extreme swing days, those most tied to health effects, are also becoming rarer. The authors note this could mean falling risk if the swing itself causes harm, and they call for clinical evidence on why calm, dry, clear days might strain the body.
plos-pone-0350666:
Asmaa Ahmad and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One statistics paper on filling gaps in seasonal data without wrecking the season's pattern. Standard gap-filling tools often flatten the repeating cycles in series like temperature records. Their framework first extracts the statistically solid periodic components of a series using a specialized bootstrap method, then feeds those components as helper information into an established multiple-imputation program.

In simulated experiments on temperature data with realistic seasonal structure, adding the periodic information cut reconstruction errors roughly in half compared with the same imputation program working without it. The authors stress the method assists existing imputation rather than replacing it. They present it as a practical upgrade for health and climate datasets where cycles carry real meaning.
plos-pone-0352766:
Abdullah Alasmary presents this 2026 PLOS One corpus study of the words of contract law. The aim is a keyword list for students and lawyers from abroad who work in legal English. The words come from a set of contract law textbooks. Alasmary chose them by how often they appear, how widely they spread, and how distinct they are from general legal writing.

The final list holds more than seven hundred words. They make up a clear slice of textbook language. Nouns dominate, at nearly half the entries. Adjectives and verbs come next. The author argues that a focused list helps teachers build lessons around the words that truly carry contract law. Generic academic lists miss the field's habits and stock phrases.
plos-pone-0346766:
Grace Semabia Kpeli and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One water study from Ghanaian towns flooded after the controlled spilling of the Akosombo and Kpong dams in late 2023. Ten months later, the team sampled rivers, ponds, wells, boreholes, and drains in four downstream communities and sequenced the bacterial DNA in each sample.

The water carried a wide cast of microbes, including organisms tied to gut infections and several hardy hospital-associated species known for drug resistance. Contamination varied sharply by place and water source, and even some groundwater sources carried high-risk organisms, with two towns worst affected. The authors say flood risk does not end when waters recede, and they call for targeted water safety work in the affected communities.
plos-pone-0351966:
Donghao Zhang, Xiaodong Yan, and Feng Shen built a better way to map how extreme losses could jump between Chinese financial firms. Standard tools for tail risk, the rare bad days that cause crises, often fail their own accuracy tests. Their method blends a factor model with flexible dependence patterns and checks itself by backtesting, comparing predicted joint crashes with what the math says should happen.

The new model failed its backtests far less often than the rival versions, with rejection rates cut by roughly half against two of them. Applied to listed Chinese financial institutions, the risk network it drew lined up with real market stress events. Regulators watching for contagion get a network map that has passed stricter honesty checks, and a clearer view of which firms sit at the web's risky center.
plos-pone-0349666:
Eva Messer and colleagues tracked a fat-regulating blood protein, ApoC3, across the stages of the common fatty liver disease now called MASLD. The protein helps govern triglycerides and is tied to heart risk, but its behavior as liver disease advances was unclear. Blood from a hundred ninety-seven patients, from simple fatty liver through scarring to liver cancer, was compared with samples from healthy donors.

ApoC3 did not simply climb with damage. It ran lower in the cirrhosis and cancer stages than in early disease or in controls, and low values traveled with other signs of advanced liver failure. That arc matters for drug developers, since new medicines aim to block this very protein: the stage of disease may decide whether lowering it further helps, harms, or misses the point entirely.
plos-pone-0351466:
A narrowed aortic valve once meant open-heart surgery for everyone. Now many patients receive a new valve through a leg artery. Anaïs Havet and colleagues traced how France used both options. They studied the years 2010 to 2022. Their data came from the national health system. The paper appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

More than two hundred fifty thousand procedures were counted. Tube-based replacement grew from about fourteen hundred cases a year. By 2022 it reached nearly seventeen thousand. Those patients were older than surgery patients. They also carried higher surgical risk scores. Surprisingly, famous trials and guideline updates showed no clear link to the growth.
plos-pone-0351766:
Swedish children who struggle mentally often cannot get help until a formal diagnosis lands. Karin Törnbom and co-authors interviewed fourteen executives, clinicians, and parents in the Västra Götaland region about this bottleneck, in this 2026 PLOS One qualitative study.

Waiting for a diagnosis was the central complaint, especially in schools and primary care, where support rules hinge on labels. Children with mixed or unusual difficulties fell through the cracks entirely. Regional differences and weak cooperation between services made care uneven. Participants pointed to earlier, lower-threshold support as the main opportunity to fix the pathway.
plos-pone-0351666:
Worn knee cartilage involves many genes, and Jing-le Zhuge and colleagues combined several public gene datasets to find the ones most tied to osteoarthritis. Their 2026 PLOS One study merged five collections of cartilage cell data and kept a sixth aside for checking.

After cleaning batch differences, the team listed genes whose activity changed in disease. Three different machine learning methods then voted on the strongest candidates, each using a different logic. The winners were checked against the spare dataset and against which immune cells appear in diseased tissue. The authors hope the shortlist points toward new drug targets and diagnostic markers.
plos-pone-0346366:
Paying one bundled price for a whole course of care sounds simple, but designing the contract is anything but. Sander Steenhuis, Jeroen van der Wolk, and Eric van der Hijden sorted the design decisions facing health insurers, in this 2026 PLOS One overview built from earlier literature.

Two reviewers independently pulled every stated choice from selected articles, then organized them across six stages of buying care. They found thirty-three decisions carrying one hundred ten possible options, from which treatments enter the bundle to how quality is checked. An expert panel tested the framework. The authors hope the map helps payers design bundles that reward value without inviting gaming.
plos-pone-0348266:
Salwa S Zghebi and co-authors evaluated England's national online diabetes self-management program, Healthy Living, in work published in 2026. The free program teaches people with type two diabetes about their condition and daily habits, but who signs up and whether it helps were unclear.

Linking program records with the national diabetes audit, the team compared people who registered with matched non users over a year. They mapped who joined, who stayed, and how health measures such as blood sugar changed. Large scale digital help only counts if people actually use it, and this check shows where the program reaches and where it falls short.
plos-pone-0350266:
Rogelio A Coronado and co-authors interviewed emergency doctors in 2026 about non drug pain treatments, from heat and movement to complementary approaches. Such options are endorsed for pain yet rarely offered in emergency departments, and provider views gate any change.

Nine physicians at one academic centre spoke in depth about current practice and what helps or blocks new options. Six themes emerged, spanning hospital systems, professional beliefs, and patient factors, and were drawn into a working model for rollout. The study's use is practical: it tells implementers which doors to push first, in a setting ruled by minutes.
plos-pone-0348766:
Woo Sub Kim and colleagues asked how ankle arthritis severity relates to how much people actually move. Activity protects the heart and metabolism, but a painful, arthritic ankle can quietly cut it off. The study reviewed two hundred sixty-two patients at a specialty foot and ankle clinic whose arthritis had reached at least a moderate stage on X-rays.

Patients reported their weekly activity on a standard questionnaire, converted into energy units, and rated their foot outcomes and pain. The analysis connected activity with arthritis stage while accounting for age, sex, body mass, and pain. If worse joints mean less movement, these patients face a double burden: joint damage plus the metabolic diseases that inactivity invites, which argues for activity support as part of ankle care.
plos-pone-0332566:
Ehud Herbst and colleagues describe a bacterial weapon that works outside the cell, a rarity among the defences bacteria aim at the viruses that infect them. A soil bacterium's secreted protein-chopping enzyme, brewed in a lab strain, cut down two related viruses even when only the used culture fluid was added to fresh virus, with no bacteria present. The fluid left many virus particles empty of their DNA.

Viruses could escape, but only by mutating a protein on their tails, the part that first grips a victim cell. Nearly all previously decoded bacterial defences act inside the cell, after invasion begins. An outside guard that damages virus particles in the open adds a new layer to the arms race, and the authors suggest such secreted guards may be common and simply overlooked.
plos-pone-0348366:
Ayumu Kojima and colleagues fed Alaska pollock protein to animals and cells to learn why this fish protein builds fast-twitch muscle so well. Blood taken about ninety minutes after eating the protein made muscle cells in dishes grow larger and contract more strongly. Levels of a gut hormone rose at the same moment. That hinted that something circulating carries the effect.

Deep surveys of muscle found thousands of proteins and hundreds of fats reshaped, with a striking rise in membranes carrying a prized omega-three fat. The diet held almost none of it. The pattern partly resembled endurance training. Fat-burning enzymes in muscle also switched on. The authors conclude the protein itself, as a high-quality building source, drives growth while quietly rewiring fat metabolism.
plos-pone-0348866:
Leo Joskowicz and co-workers train deep learning models to spot inherited eye diseases from wide pictures of the retina. These diseases, passed through families, can be slow to diagnose. Their 2026 study uses records from an Israeli medical center covering just over four hundred patients, pairing two kinds of eye images with genetic test results.

Models given both image types did best at telling diseased eyes from healthy ones. They also sorted patients into groups of likely faulty genes with good accuracy. Results held up across repeated rounds of checking. Image-based screening of this kind could point patients toward the right genetic tests sooner, saving time in clinics that lack eye-genetics experts.
plos-pone-0348566:
Qiu Jie and co-workers ask how social media use connects with exercise habits among older adults in China. Phones and apps now bring seniors health news and social contact. Their 2026 study surveys more than eleven hundred people aged sixty and over, measuring media use, coping style, felt support from others, and exercise habits in one snapshot.

Media use linked with more active coping and stronger felt support, and both of those linked with better exercise habits. The path ran in a chain: media use fed coping, coping fed felt support, and support helped lock in exercise. The authors suggest programs that use social platforms to build confidence and community could help older adults stay active.
plos-pone-0346666:
Tomasz Piróg and colleagues analysed more than fifty-five thousand Polish-language posts on X, formerly Twitter, from the first year of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Poland took in huge numbers of Ukrainian refugees, and social media framed what the public made of them. The 2026 study combined frame analysis with stance detection, network mapping, and engagement measures.

Negative posts were the most numerous, at about sixty percent, yet positive posts spread furthest per post. Government supporters and the liberal opposition both leaned pro-Ukrainian, while a nationalist cluster criticised the arrivals but reached few people. A smaller mixed group stayed neutral. The authors show how framing and network structure together shape crisis debates.
plos-pone-0348066:
Madeleine I. R. Brodbeck and colleagues asked whether a brain region called Cluster N, linked to magnetic compass sensing in migrating birds, also switches on in zebra finches, which do not migrate. Finches searched for food in a maze under three magnetic conditions: one honest field pointing to the food, and two scrambled fields carrying no direction. Afterwards the team stained brains for a gene that marks recent activity.

Activity rose in both Cluster N and the hippocampus, the brain's map room, but equally under all three field conditions. That gives no firm proof Cluster N reads the compass here. Still, its presence and activation in a non-migrant hints the region serves broader orientation jobs.
plos-pone-0347866:
Hamed Tabesh and co-authors built hybrid forecasters for the daily flood of patients into an emergency department, a number managers must predict to staff safely. Weather and calendar effects make arrivals bend in both straight-line and curved patterns. Their 2026 study blended a classic time-series method with a neural network in two architectures, then raced them against five rival approaches at several forecast horizons.

The second hybrid, which merged the two methods' forecasts, won overall, especially in the volatile middle horizon where single models stumbled. The extended statistical model did best at calm, long horizons. The authors offer emergency departments a practical recipe matched to forecast distance and turbulence.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Mongolia's road to the UN took sixteen years of Cold War bargaining. The landlocked state had applied repeatedly since 1946. Great-power vetoes blocked it each time. A package deal finally cleared the way in 1961. Resolution 166 was adopted on 25 October 1961 by nine votes to none. The United States abstained.

The Council recommended the Mongolian People's Republic for admission. The Assembly seated Mongolia two days later. Mauritania entered in the same bargain. Washington disliked recognizing a Soviet ally. It let the vote pass anyway, swallowing its doubts. This resolution thus marks a rare Cold War compromise: two locked doors opened together, widening the UN toward true universality.

Fresh war broke out in south Palestine days before 1949. Shots had rung out on 22 December 1948. The stand-in mediator sent word of the clash. Resolution 66 passed on 29 December 1948 by eight votes to none. Three states held back, the two Soviet bloc teams and the United States among them.

Both sides had to call an instant halt to the guns. Old truce terms from November had to be put in force. UN men had to watch the truce in full, with free range. A Council team would meet at Lake Success on 7 January 1949. It would weigh how far each side had obeyed. Cuba and Norway would join the team from New Year. The new peace talks body, set up that month, was urged to start work fast.

On 8 October 2004 the Council passed Resolution 1566 by a full vote. It hones the Council's words on terror. All states must fight terror by all means the Charter and world law allow, it says once more. It voices deep alarm at the growth in the slain, children among them. Hate and zealotry drive more and more of the attacks, in land after land. States were told to work in full with the Council's three anti-terror teams. Those teams, in turn, must work as one.

The text reached past the known foes as well. A team was set up to draft real bars, such as bans on trips and frozen funds, for terror-linked men and groups past Al-Qaida and the Taliban. Law binds this fight too, the Council stressed.

Resolution 366, adopted unanimously on 17 December 1974, condemns South Africa's grip on Namibia in the bluntest terms yet. The Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a UN council for the territory; the World Court ruled in 1971 that South Africa was obliged to withdraw. Pretoria answered with continued occupation, brutal repression of Namibians, and moves to break the territory's unity through ethnic homelands.

The Council condemned the illegal occupation and the persistent refusal to obey the Assembly, the Council, and the court's opinion. It condemned the repression and human rights violations as well. It demanded that South Africa withdraw its administration and stop carving up the territory, steps toward the free Namibia the UN had promised since the 1960s.

Resolution 1466, adopted on 14 March 2003, keeps the Ethiopia-Eritrea peace process moving toward marking the border. The Boundary Commission had issued its ruling on the line in April 2002, and both sides had accepted it as final. Prisoners of war had been sent home, and the UN Mission in Ethiopia and Eritrea, UNMEE, was in place as the marking phase drew near.

The Council extends UNMEE until 15 September 2003. It urges both countries to work with the Boundary Commission, follow its marking directions, and give its field staff safety on the ground. It voices worry about crossings into the Temporary Security Zone and new anti-tank mines there. It also demands full freedom of movement for UNMEE and notes drought and hunger pressing on both countries.

Preventing wars before they start is the theme of Resolution 1366, adopted unanimously on 30 August 2001. The Council had before it the Secretary-General's report on the prevention of armed conflict, with ten principles and proposals for a system-wide strategy. It recalled the failures that preceded the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre, and the threat from illicit small arms flows.

The Council declares conflict prevention an integral part of its core duty. It stresses that primary responsibility rests with national governments, with the UN in support. It promises prompt attention to early warnings from the Secretary-General under Article 99, more Council missions to tension areas, and preventive deployment with host consent. It backs fact-finding missions, regional prevention strategies, and stronger prevention capacity in bodies such as the OAU and ECOWAS. Peacekeeping mandates should include disarmament and child-soldier rehabilitation where fitting.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: The General Assembly adopted Resolution 69/66 at its sixty-ninth session in 2014. It decides to convene the Third Conference of States Parties and Signatories to Treaties that Establish Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones and Mongolia. The one-day conference is set for New York in 2015. Its purpose is to examine ways of strengthening cooperation among the zones and with Mongolia. The treaties' parties recognize Mongolia's single-state nuclear-weapon-free status alongside their own arrangements.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended on 31 March 2006, and the terms for settling the Abkhazia conflict are restated. The work of the Secretary-General's Special Representative, helped by Russia as facilitator and by the Group of Friends, is backed. UNOMIG and the CIS peacekeeping force together kept the conflict zone stable.

Any settlement, the Council insists, must come by peaceful means within Georgia's recognized borders. Both sides are called on to finish a package of documents on non-use of force and refugee return without delay. Georgia is urged to take Abkhaz security concerns seriously, and the Abkhaz leadership to face the need for a dignified return of displaced people and respect for their rights.

Somalia's arms embargo Monitoring Group is extended on 23 July 2007. The group had been renewed in stages since 2003, most recently that February alongside the authorization of the African Union mission. The embargo's carve-out for supplies meant only to build Somalia's security sector is recalled in detail.

The group's mandate is extended for a further period so it can keep gathering evidence of embargo violations and report through the sanctions committee. Somalia's transitional institutions, it is stressed, must keep working toward effective national governance. The renewal kept independent eyes on arms flows into Somalia at a moment when a new regional force was deploying and the security picture was shifting fast.

Georgia's United Nations mission is extended on 13 February 2009, after the August 2008 war. A six-point agreement of 12 August 2008 and follow-up measures of 8 September had set the ceasefire terms. Geneva discussions between the sides had begun in October, and the Secretary-General's February report proposed a revised security regime for the conflict zones.

The August and September arrangements are recalled, and respect for the 1994 Moscow ceasefire's separation-of-forces rules is called for until a new security regime is agreed. Avoiding force and any ethnic discrimination is stressed, and free humanitarian access is demanded. The mission's mandate is extended for a new period, and the Secretary-General is asked to report on how the parties are carrying out the resolution.

The war crimes courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda were both winding down in 2010. On 22 December that year the Council adopted Resolution 1966. It created a new body, the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. Some work would still remain after the two courts closed. Fugitive trials, appeals, and witness protection all needed a home.

The Mechanism was designed as a small, temporary body with two branches. The Rwanda branch would start work on 1 July 2012. The Yugoslavia branch would start on 1 July 2013. From those dates, the Mechanism would take over the courts' remaining duties and legal powers. The Council told both courts to finish all their remaining work by the end of 2014. They also had to prepare a smooth handover of files and tasks.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force was still needed in 1969, even though the island had grown calmer. The Secretary-General reported that recent improvements had held. Cyprus agreed that the force should stay beyond 15 June 1969. Resolution 266 was adopted unanimously on 10 June 1969.

The Council reaffirmed its earlier Cyprus resolutions. It urged the parties to act with the utmost restraint and to make good use of the calmer climate. The force's stay was extended for a further period ending on 15 December 1969. The Council expected that enough progress toward a final solution would be made by then. Such progress might allow the force to withdraw, or at least to be cut down.

Food for civilians sat inside the sanctions on Iraq in 1990, with one gate left open for cases of real need. The embargo of Resolution 661 covered food, except in humanitarian circumstances. Several member states had written to the sanctions committee about the food situation in Iraq and Kuwait. Resolution 666 set out how that need would be judged.

The Council decided that its sanctions committee would keep the food situation under constant review. Aid agencies had to report urgently on conditions. Children under fifteen, expectant mothers, the sick, and the elderly needed special attention. If the committee found an urgent humanitarian need, it would report to the Council at once. Food could then be supplied through the United Nations, working with the Red Cross or other aid bodies. The text also noted that medical supplies were not covered by the embargo.
un-sc-res-66:
Fighting broke out again in south Palestine in December 1948. The acting mediator sent word of the new clashes, which began on 22 December. On 29 December 1948 the Council called for a fast ceasefire. The governments had to use resolution 61 without more delay. That text told forces to pull back to their October lines. The mediator's orders under it also had to be obeyed.

United Nations observers needed full freedom to watch the truce on the ground. The Council wanted the truce checked in full. Its call came as talks on Rhodes were about to open. Those talks led to the 1949 truce deals. This text helped push the sides toward them.
un-sc-res-1566:
Terrorism's definition and reach were pressed forward on 8 October 2004. Beslan and other attacks had swollen the count of victims, children among them. The Council restated resolutions 1267 (1999), 1373 (2001), and 1540 (2004). It reminded states that every counter-terrorism step had to honor human rights, refugee, and humanitarian law. Its three counter-terrorism bodies were told to work more closely together.

The Council condemned all acts of terrorism in the strongest terms, whatever their motive, wherever and by whomsoever committed. It recalled that crimes meant to kill or maim civilians, or to take hostages in order to terrorize a public, can never be justified. States were called to join every anti-terrorism convention as a matter of urgency. They had to speed agreement on the draft comprehensive convention on terrorism. A working group was set up to weigh practical measures against groups and persons outside the Al-Qaida sanctions list.
un-sc-res-366:
Namibia's occupier was given a deadline to declare itself on 17 December 1974. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966 and set up a Council for Namibia. The World Court's 1971 opinion held that South Africa must withdraw. Pretoria still refused and ruled the territory by force. Its repression of Namibians and its racial laws drew the Council's anger.

The Council condemned the continued illegal occupation of Namibia. It condemned the racial and repressive laws South Africa applied there. South Africa had to make a solemn declaration that it would obey the United Nations decisions and the Court's opinion. It then had to take the steps needed to withdraw and hand power to the Namibian people. The Council would meet on or before 30 May 1975 to review South Africa's compliance and weigh the next steps.
un-sc-res-1466:
UNMEE was extended as demarcation approached on 14 March 2003. Prisoners of war had been freed and sent home by both sides. Crossings of the Temporary Security Zone's southern edge caused concern. The Boundary Commission's ruling of 13 April 2002 awaited marking on the ground. The peace process was about to enter its decisive phase, the Council noted.

The Council extended UNMEE to 15 September 2003, at the troop and observer levels set by resolution 1320 (2000). Both parties were urged to meet their Algiers duties and to work with the Red Cross on the questions left open. They had to work fully and swiftly with UNMEE and give it complete freedom of movement. Every limit on the mission had to go at once. The Council backed UNMEE's power to check the parties' conduct inside the zone. Mine action work by the mission was also praised.
un-sc-res-1366:
Action on preventing armed conflict came with Resolution 1366, adopted on 30 August 2001. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a full report on prevention. Its lessons drew on failed efforts before the Rwanda genocide and the Srebrenica massacre. Small arms flows kept making wars worse and longer.

The Council vows to treat prevention as a core part of its work. It will watch danger spots closely and act early, with missions to tense regions where states agree. The Secretary-General should flag threats, rights abuses, and disputes that could turn violent. Peacekeeping mandates may add disarmament work and police for the peace that follows. Regional bodies, above all in Africa, need more capacity and funds.
europmc-pmc10957466:
Marin and a large team tested a ready-made cell therapy for blood cancers in this 2024 trial report. Natural killer cells are immune cells that kill infected or cancerous cells. The team fitted such cells, taken from donated cord blood, with a sensor that targets a marker called CD19 on B cell tumours. The cells also carried a growth signal called interleukin-15. Thirty-seven patients with B cell cancers took part.

No severe side effects such as cytokine release syndrome or graft-versus-host disease appeared, the team reports. Half the patients, 48.6 percent, had responded by day 30, and the rate held at day 100. One year after treatment, 68 percent were alive. Responses were strongest when the cord blood had few red cell precursors and was frozen within 24 hours of collection. Those best units yielded cells rich in attack genes.
europmc-pmc10958066:
Deng and colleagues give a full account of one key growth signal in health and disease in this 2024 review. TGF-beta is a signal protein made by nearly every tissue and cell type. Its signals guide embryo growth, wound healing, and the day-to-day balance of tissues and the immune system. When the signal goes wrong, it can drive disease instead.

The review retraces the field's history and explains how the protein is made, switched on, and passed into cells. It then details what the signal does in healthy states and in illness. Therapies that target the signal are highlighted, since they have brought new options for linked diseases. The authors aim to give readers one systematic map of the whole topic. They also flag where fresh work is most needed.
europmc-pmc11405266:
Argentieri and a large team build a blood protein clock that estimates biological age in this 2024 study. Plasma proteins can potentially measure how fast a person is ageing, beyond years lived. The team developed the clock in the UK Biobank with 45,441 people, using a platform that measures 2,897 plasma proteins. They then tested its use for predicting disease and death in diverse populations.

A set of 204 proteins predicted chronological age with a correlation of 0.94, they report. Faster proteomic ageing tracked with 18 major chronic diseases, including heart, liver, kidney, and lung diseases, diabetes, brain degeneration, and cancer. It also tracked with having several diseases at once and with all-cause mortality. Links appeared with telomere length, frailty, and reaction time. Top clock proteins act in matrix structure, immunity, inflammation, and hormone pathways.
europmc-pmc11880366:
Xiao and co-authors surveyed peptide drugs in a 2025 review. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins. They can act as precise drugs for many diseases. Weak points include fast breakdown in the body.

New design methods and smart delivery systems now ease those faults. Peptides treat diabetes, weight gain, cancer, and rare diseases. They also serve as vaccine parts and as guided carriers. Xiao tracks market growth and trials in progress. Artificial intelligence now speeds the search for useful peptides. It appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy.
europmc-pmc1247566:
Bornehag and colleagues linked house dust phthalates to child allergy symptoms in 2004. Allergy and asthma rates in children had climbed for three decades. Dust was sampled in homes of 198 symptomatic children. A matched set of 202 symptom-free children served as controls.

One phthalate, BBzP, ran higher in case homes, at 0.15 versus 0.12 milligrams per gram. BBzP tied to runny nose and eczema symptoms. Another, DEHP, tied to asthma instead. Each child got clinical and home technical checks. Bornehag shows indoor chemical dust may track with lasting allergy. Cases and controls came from a wider cohort of 10,852 children in Sweden.
europmc-pmc1253666:
Nash and colleagues exposed zebrafish to a potent hormone drug across generations in 2004. Ethynylestradiol is a birth control drug found in waterways. It acts at very low concentrations in fish. Breeding groups were kept on realistic water levels for life.

Lifelong exposure at 5 nanograms per liter cut egg output by 56 percent. That generation then failed fully, with no fertilization at all. Males lacked working testes and showed disturbed sex development. By contrast, 40 days of exposure in adult parents caused no harm. Nash proves life-stage timing decides the damage. The harm thus skipped the first group and struck the next generation in full.
europmc-pmc1318466:
Akins, Tolson, and Cole tested expert panel stability with bootstrap methods in 2005. Delphi surveys poll experts in rounds to reach consensus. No rule fixed how many experts a panel needs. The test case was a first-round survey of 23 health quality experts.

Responses covered 54 survey items on hospital excellence criteria. Bootstrap sampling expanded the data to two larger fake panels. Means, trimmed means, spread, and confidence ranges were compared. First-round data were chosen for their widest diversity. Akins checks whether small panel results hold up when virtually enlarged. In the end, the small panel's answers stayed stable under both larger fake panels.
europmc-pmc1564166:
When SARS struck in 2002, doctors had no tested treatments. Stockman, Bellamy, and Garner reviewed all treatment studies in 2006 for the World Health Organization. They covered ribavirin, steroids, two HIV drugs, interferon, antibodies, and patient plasma.

In lab dishes, ribavirin, lopinavir, and interferon slowed the virus. In patients, proof was far weaker. Of 26 ribavirin studies, all were inconclusive or flagged possible harm. Of 29 steroid studies, four suggested harm. Plasma and antibody studies were also inconclusive. Stockman concludes no treatment had proven benefit, a stark brief for future outbreaks. Strong trial proof was missing throughout.
europmc-pmc2000966: A single mutation in the PB1-F2 of H5N1 (HK/97) and 1918 influenza A viruses contributes to increased virulence. — a 2005 science paper on a flu mutation raising harm. It finds the single mutation. The paper is the mutation study: the findings on influenza, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2022666: DDT and breast cancer in young women: new data on the significance of age at exposure. — a 2005 science paper on DDT and breast cancer. It studies the exposure-age link. The paper is the DDT study: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2248166: Quantitative peptide binding motifs for 19 human and mouse MHC class I molecules derived using positional scanning combinatorial peptide libraries. — a 2005 science paper on peptide binding motifs. It derives the binding motifs. The paper is the motif study: the findings on MHC ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2361666: The safety and feasibility of extracorporeal high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) for the t — a 2008 science paper on HIFU safety. It tests the HIFU safety. The paper is the safety study: the findings on ultrasound ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2375266: Activation of AKT/PKB in breast cancer predicts a worse outcome among endocrine treated patient — a 2008 science paper on AKT in breast cancer. It predicts the worse outcome. The paper is the prediction study: the findings on breast ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2519166: The dynamic brain: from spiking neurons to neural masses and cortical fields. — a 2008 science paper on modeling the dynamic brain. It moves from spiking neurons to fields. The paper is the brain study: the findings on neurons, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2568866: Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel smoke is a major health concern in the developing world. — a 2008 science paper on indoor air pollution. It flags the biomass-smoke concern. The paper is the concern study: the findings on pollution ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2627866: The 2006 California heat wave: impacts on hospitalizations and emergency department visits. — a 2008 science paper on the 2006 California heat wave. It measures the hospitalization impacts. The paper is the impact study: the findings on heat ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2658866: Combined impact of lifestyle factors on mortality: prospective cohort study in US women. — a 2008 science paper on habit bundles and death rates. It measures the habit-bundle impact for labs. The paper is the impact study: the notes on habit ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2683166: Measuring the activity of BioBrick promoters using an in vivo reference standard. — a 2008 science paper on BioBrick starter gauges. It gauges the starters for labs. The paper is the gauge study: the notes on BioBrick ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2698066: Lrig1 expression defines a distinct multipotent stem cell population in mammalian epidermis. — a 2008 science paper on Lrig1 stem cells. It defines the multipotent population. The paper is the Lrig1 study: the findings on stem ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2745766: Community-wide analysis of microbial genome sequence signatures. — a 2008 science paper on bug-crowd gene tags. It reads the gene tags for labs. The paper is the tag study: the notes on bug ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2762766: Infodemiology and infoveillance: framework for an emerging set of public health informatics met — a 2008 science paper on web-health spy tools. It frames the web-health tools for labs. The paper is the tool study: the notes on web ills, filed here in full session today.
mahhabone-1766:
Mahhabone, printed in London in 1766, promises to open the Grand Lodge door. The anonymous exposé covers the three Craft degrees and adds the Royal Arch beside them. That addition gives the pamphlet its scholarly weight today, as early printed evidence for how the Royal Arch degree was worked in the 1760s.

The title is itself one of the Craft's guarded words, printed for every reader to see. Ritual questions and answers carry the candidate through each degree. Exposés like this one sold because lodges would not speak for themselves. Mahhabone preserves forms that official Masonry left unrecorded. Historians of the Royal Arch treat the little book as a key witness.
hiram-grand-master-key-1766:
Hiram, or the Grand Master-Key, appeared in London in 1766 under the byline of a member of the Royal Arch. The exposé covers both Antient and Modern masonry. That double coverage makes it a pivotal witness to the rival rituals of the Masonic schism, the great split that divided the English Craft in the eighteenth century.

Two competing Masonries stand weighed in a single key. Their words, signs, and charges differ in ways the pamphlet sets side by side. Readers of 1766 could compare what the lodges kept apart. Historians still use Hiram to date and distinguish the two workings. The Grand Master-Key unlocks less a door than a quarrel, and preserves both sides of it.
plos-pone-0004966:
Electrical impulses coordinate movement, secretion and sensing in animals. Many of those signals are fast action potentials based on sodium. Alison Taylor reported an unexpected case in PLOS ONE in 2009. She studied a marine diatom, a single-celled alga. The diatom fired fast electrical spikes of its own.

The diatom's action potential is based on sodium and calcium together. That makes it much like an animal nerve impulse. Finding it in plankton pushes the roots of electrical signaling deep into evolution. Excitability is not an animal invention. Even a drifting alga can spark, which raises new questions about what such spikes do for the cell.
plos-pone-0005066:
Soybeans battle a water mold called Phytophthora sojae. The mold attacks roots and ruins harvests. Dinah Qutob and colleagues studied two of its weapon genes. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The genes are Avr1a and Avr3a. Plants can recognize these genes' products and resist. The mold evolves to escape recognition.

The study found copy number variation in both genes. The mold duplicates or drops copies to dodge plant defenses. It also varies how strongly the genes are transcribed. That double game reveals an arms race at the DNA level. Breeders can use the knowledge. Knowing how the mold escapes helps them design resistance that lasts longer.
plos-pone-0005166:
Many pregnant women in the United States skip HIV testing. Shorter pre-test counseling had raised testing uptake. Deborah Cohan and colleagues compared the two counseling styles in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their trial ran in the prenatal setting. It was randomized and designed as a non-inferiority test. Patient perspectives were the focus.

Abbreviated counseling held its own against standard counseling. Patients' decision-making and satisfaction were measured. Shorter sessions did not leave women worse informed. That supports simpler counseling to get more mothers tested. Testing in pregnancy prevents transmission to babies. Removing friction from testing saves lives. The study checks that simplification does not cost patients anything important.
plos-pone-0005266:
Smell begins in tiny cilia where odor signals flood the cell with calcium. That calcium must be cleared fast, before it reaches toxic levels. Kleene studied the pump that does the clearing in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The pump, called the plasma membrane calcium ATPase, moves calcium out of the olfactory cilium. The study probed the limits of how much calcium it can clear. Knowing the ceiling explains how smell cells reset after each sniff and where that reset can fail. Smell fades when this pump can no longer keep up, so the limits found here may help explain some losses of smell that come with age or illness.
plos-pone-0005366:
Streptococcus pyogenes, the strep throat bacterium, coats its wall with a component that carries D-alanine. Mutations in the dlt machinery change that coating and reduce virulence in many species. Cox and colleagues switched off the DltA gene in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Inactivating DltA modulated how the bacterium expresses its virulence factors, as the title states. The wall change was thought to work by exposing the germ to antimicrobial peptides. Showing wider effects on virulence genes reframes how this surface tweak tames the pathogen. The wall of this germ is its first touch with the throat, so a change there shifts each step that comes next. From sticking to the wall to the sore and fever a child feels at home.
plos-pone-0005966:
HIV harms the antibody arm of the immune system early, and treatment does not fully repair it. Sandrine Peruchon, Nada Chaoul, Chantal Burelout and colleagues studied that early harm in 2009 using SIV, the monkey form of the virus. Their PLOS ONE paper follows B cells, the cells that make antibodies, in blood and in tissues during acute infection.

Memory B cells, which hold the record of past fights, were broadly lost, and the loss differed by tissue. Damage done this early may set the course of the whole disease. The work shows why the first weeks of infection deserve close study, and why a vaccine will need to guard B cells before the virus can thin their ranks.
plos-pone-0006066:
A fatty diet loads the liver with fat, and strangely also switches on fat-making genes there. Maaike Oosterveer, Theo van Dijk, Uwe Tietge and colleagues asked in 2009 whether those genes truly raise the flow of new fat. Their PLOS ONE paper feeds mice a high-fat diet and measures fatty acid elongation in the liver directly.

The title confirms real induction: the liver lengthens fatty acids more under the diet. Gene switches alone can mislead, so measuring the actual flux settles the paradox. The result matters for fatty liver disease, a growing burden, since it shows the liver under a fatty diet is not just storing fat but actively reshaping it.
plos-pone-0006166:
Fruit and nut trees need a dose of winter cold before they will bloom well in spring. Eike Luedeling, Minghua Zhang and Evan Girvetz mapped that dose across California, past and future, in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper tracks winter chill from 1950 to 2099 using two different chilling models, since chill defines where many tree crops can be grown.

Chill is declining across that span, the title reports, under both models. A tree planted for a thirty-year life may outlive the climate it was chosen for. The maps give growers and planners a hard basis for shifting crops and regions before orchards fail, rather than after.
plos-pone-0006266:
Guessing a protein's job from its letter sequence works for fewer than half of newly found proteins. Torgeir Hvidsten and colleagues tested shape as an alternative clue in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Structural genomics raised hopes that similar local shapes would imply similar functions.

The team ran a comprehensive analysis of structure and function based on local structure similarity. Comparing small shape patches can link distant proteins that sequences cannot. Better function guesses speed up genome annotation everywhere. The work weighs how far shape alone can carry those guesses. Readers gain a clear view of how shape can hint at what a protein does.
plos-pone-0006666:
Kok Keng Tee and co-authors isolated a working molecular clone of a recombinant HIV-1 form in PLOS ONE in 2009. A growing number of emerging HIV-1 recombinants classified as circulating recombinant forms have been identified in Southeast Asia in recent years. Recombinants arise when two viral strains mix in one person. The team established a molecular clone of one such form.

Their title reports the clone is replication-competent: it can copy itself in culture. A working clone lets labs study the recombinant's biology precisely. Regional HIV diversity matters for vaccine design and diagnostics. Southeast Asian forms are an important part of that picture.
plos-pone-0006766:
Fiona D. Barr and co-authors studied how arsenic switches off stress-hormone genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Long-term exposure to inorganic arsenic is a worldwide health risk. It is linked to effects from cancer to diabetes. It also affects reproduction. The authors focused on genes controlled by the glucocorticoid receptor. That receptor manages stress and metabolism signals.

Arsenic disrupted histone modification at those genes' promoters. It also blocked recruitment of a partner protein called CARM1. Without those steps, transcription was repressed. The mechanism connects an environmental poison to gene control directly. It may explain several of arsenic's varied health effects at once.
plos-pone-0006866:
Johan Ursing and his team tracked drug-proof malaria germs through the year in PLOS ONE in 2009. A gene mark called pfcrt 76T flags proof against chloroquine. Germs with the mark are spread wide through Africa. In Guinea-Bissau, a double dose of chloroquine still beat a plain dose by far. The ask was if drug use piles up proof as the year turns.

The title gives the reply: no such pile-up was seen. Heavy use of the high dose did not stack proof through the seasons. That counts where chloroquine is still in use. Dose plans may keep a cheap drug of use for longer. Proof must still be watched as long as the drug is used.
plos-pone-0006966:
Flávia Mury, José Roberto da Silva, Ligia Ferreira, and colleagues studied blood digestion in a biting bug in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rhodnius prolixus feeds on blood and must handle large amounts of hemoglobin. Digestion frees heme, which is toxic in loose form. The bug detoxifies heme by packing it into crystals called hemozoin.

The team found an enzyme, alpha-glucosidase, helps form those crystals. They place the finding in an evolutionary story about blood feeders. Turning poison into inert crystal is a neat survival trick. Blocking it could one day offer a way to control this insect, which spreads Chagas disease.
plos-pone-0007066:
Ana Rivas-Caicedo, Gloria Soldevila, Teresa Fortoul, and colleagues studied an immune enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. Dendritic cells must mature and travel to lymph nodes to start immune responses. The signal receptor CCR7 guides that travel. The team had earlier shown the enzyme Jak3 helps CCR7 signaling in T lymphocytes.

Using mice that lack Jak3, they tested dendritic cells directly. Jak3 proved involved in both maturation and CCR7-driven migration. Without it, the cells' homing suffered. The finding ties a known immune defect gene to the cells that launch immune responses.
plos-pone-0007166:
Jung Hwan Kim, Min Ki Jee, So Young Lee, and colleagues studied stem-like genes in fat tissue cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adipose tissue stromal cells are adult cells from fat. Oct4 is a transcription factor famous for marking embryonic stem cells. Whether it works in these adult fat cells was unclear. The team examined how Oct4 expression is controlled there.

They also tracked other embryonic genes in fully differentiated cells. Then they measured how endogenous Oct4 levels steer cell behavior. Even traces of this factor may keep adult cells more flexible. That flexibility is prized for regenerative medicine using a patient's own fat.
plos-pone-0007266:
Karine H. Hellemans, Jean-Claude Hannaert, Bart Denys, and colleagues studied how fatty acids harm insulin-producing cells in 2009. Chronically high fatty acid levels can kill pancreatic beta cells in the lab. Individual beta cells vary in how sensitive they are to that toxicity, even within the same culture.

Earlier rat work linked resistance to fat storage and mitochondrial handling. The authors examine a fat-regulating enzyme controlled by the LXR and PPARalpha pathways. They report that this enzyme regulates beta cell susceptibility to fatty acids. Their finding may guide efforts to protect beta cells in type 2 diabetes.
plos-pone-0007366:
Hossein Khiabanian, Vladimir Trifonov, and Raul Rabadan analyzed gene swapping in swine influenza viruses in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Three human influenza pandemics occurred in the twentieth century. Pandemic strains emerge from non-human reservoirs where humans have little or no immunity to the new virus combinations that form there.

At least two pandemic strains arose through reassortment, where viruses swap gene segments. The authors study reassortment patterns in swine influenza viruses. Pigs are a key mixing host for flu. Their patterns help scientists judge how new pandemic strains might assemble.
openalex-w1916572066: Climate change threatens crops — breeding must keep up. Kole and colleagues' 2015 Frontiers in Plant Science review surveys genomics-assisted breeding for climate resilient crops. The review charted the progress and prospects of DNA-guided breeding for a warming world.
openalex-w1931066666: Nearly 300 single-gene immune errors are now known. A 2015 paper by Bousfiha and colleagues presents the IUIS classification for primary immunodeficiencies. The system organized the disorders by their clinical patterns across five broad groups.
openalex-w2097847166: HIV subtypes differ — treatment must account for it. A 2005 global study tracked how HIV-1 subtype and drug therapy shape protease and RT genes. The work mapped resistance mutations across diverse viruses worldwide — a guide for doctors.
plos-pone-0006366:
When did the peoples of Africa first grow fast in number? Murray Cox and his team read DNA from foraging and farming groups south of the Sahara in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. One view ties growth to new tools made by hunters in the Late Stone Age; a later view ties it to the spread of farms.

The DNA bears signs of growth that reach back to the Late Stone Age, well before farms spread. Growth thus seems to have begun with Stone Age hunters, not with crops. That moves the start of the boom back by a long span. The work gives a firmer past for the peoples of the region.
openalex-w2253274866: City air is full of fine particles — and lungs pay the price. This 2016 Frontiers in Immunology review surveys what six decades of evidence say about air pollutants and severe respiratory disease, with a focus on particulate matter. The authors break down how particle composition drives harm, connecting what is in the air to what happens in the airways.
openalex-w2738161666: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus spread five major viruses — chikungunya, dengue, Rift Valley fever, yellow fever, and Zika. This 2017 PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases paper reviews the contemporary status of insecticide resistance in these mosquitoes. As resistance spreads, the review warns, the chemical tools of mosquito control are losing their edge.
openalex-w2765824866: This 2017 article in Educar em Revista (in Portuguese) discusses 'Becoming Critical' — the landmark book by Wilfred Carr and Stephen Kemmis that shaped action research and collaborative inquiry in education. With over thirty years of influence, the book's call to make educational research critical and emancipatory remains, the piece argues, urgently relevant.
openalex-w2789006266: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations raise cancer risk worldwide — but most data came from white Europeans and North Americans. This 2018 Human Mutation paper, from the CIMBA consortium's 18,435 families, maps the mutational spectrum across 29,700 families globally. The worldwide view reveals how mutation patterns — and the risks they carry — vary by ancestry.
openalex-w2922904366: Beach water and sewage harbor microbial communities — including reservoirs of antibiotic resistance. This 2019 Microbiome paper uses metagenomics to uncover resistance reservoirs in coastal beach and sewage waters. The findings map an environmental dimension of the resistance crisis that flows straight into public health.
openalex-w3005664566: Since 2013, the IUIS expert committee has published an updated phenotypic classification of inborn errors of immunity. This 2020 Journal of Clinical Immunology paper presents the 2019 update — ten tables complementing the genotypic classification. The catalog remains the clinical reference for these rare disorders.
openalex-w3021969666: Countries pledged climate action — but are their policies enough? This 2020 Nature Communications paper takes stock of national climate policies to evaluate Paris Agreement implementation, ahead of the 2023 global stocktake. The assessment measures the combined effort against the temperature goals.
europmc-pmc2814866: Fat tissue is not just storage, it is active biology, and this 2010 paper profiles its microRNA regulators. The authors map miRNA expression in human subcutaneous fat and track how it changes as fat cells mature. The profile reveals which tiny RNAs steer fat development. The data became a resource for obesity and metabolism research.
europmc-pmc2815666: A companion to the XDS paper, this 2010 article by Wolfgang Kabsch covers the next steps in crystallography data processing. It explains integration, scaling, space-group assignment, and post-refinement, the stages that convert raw measurements into accurate data. The paper is a practical guide to getting the numbers right. Together with XDS, it standardized a field.
europmc-pmc2831066: The amyloid beta protein blamed in Alzheimer's may have a day job fighting germs. This 2010 paper reports that it acts as an antimicrobial peptide, killing microbes in lab tests. The authors propose its brain buildup might start as immune defense gone wrong. The provocative finding reframed a notorious molecule as part of innate immunity.
europmc-pmc2851566: One DNA patch, 9p21, kept turning up in diseases from heart trouble to tumors. This 2010 paper ties its SNPs to many disease forms and links them to ANRIL, a nearby RNA. The team bared a shared root. The find hinted one patch may steer several diseases.
europmc-pmc2897766: Cells tune their stress response with exquisite care. This 2010 paper shows BiP binding to the stress sensor Ire1 tunes the unfolded protein response's homeostatic behavior. The authors' quantitative work reveals the dial. Their finding matters for diseases of protein misfolding.
europmc-pmc2911766: Surgery patients do better when fluids are tuned, not poured. This 2010 randomized study tests fluid tuning with stroke volume variation in high-risk surgery patients. The authors show guided fluids beat fixed doses. Their result changed how anesthesia teams handle fluids.
europmc-pmc3013466: Disgust evolved to keep us from disease. This 2011 paper argues the yuck response is a disease-avoidance system. The authors make the evolutionary case. Their work reframed a basic emotion. Rotten smells trigger the ancient alarm. Moral disgust may borrow the same wiring.
europmc-pmc3111466: Wheat fiber fed good gut bugs in fat mice. This 2011 paper shows wheat arabinoxylan boosts bifidobacteria and friends in obese mice. The authors link fiber to flora. Their work backs prebiotics. Weight gain slowed on the fiber diet. Whole grains may work the same way.
europmc-pmc3136466: A plant pathogen's evolution got sequenced. This 2011 paper compares 19 Pseudomonas syringae genomes to trace pathogenicity's evolution. The authors reveal rapid weapon swaps. Their work aids crop defense. Effector genes jumped between strains. Breeders race to match the swaps. The study is a genomics landmark.
europmc-pmc3156766: Africa's diabetes surge got mapped. This 2011 review tracks diabetes across sub-Saharan Africa from 1999 to 2011. The authors reveal the steep rise. Their work guides public health. Cities carried the heaviest burden. Clinics lack insulin, they warn. The review spurred funding drives.
europmc-pmc3185266: Infections after stroke got pooled. This 2011 meta-analysis measures how often infection strikes after stroke. The authors confirm the heavy burden. Their work guides prevention. Pneumonia led the infections, they found. Preventive antibiotics remain debated. Stroke units now watch for fever.
europmc-pmc3218866: A fungus's fungus-eating past got confirmed. This 2011 paper shows mycoparasitism was Trichoderma's ancestral lifestyle. The authors compare the genomes. Their work guides biocontrol. Modern strains still eat other fungi. Farmers deploy them as biocontrol. The paper shaped fungal biology.
europmc-pmc3267166: A tumor-starving drug got a design review. This 2010 paper traces cilengitide's design, synthesis, and trials. The authors map the path. Their overview guides pharma. The drug starved tumors of blood. Trials tested it in brain cancer. Kessler's lab led the work.
europmc-pmc3314666: A flu shot got a narcolepsy link. This 2012 paper links Finland's H1N1 vaccine to a spike in childhood narcolepsy. The authors reveal the increase. Their work shaped vaccine safety. Risk rose twelvefold, they found. Nohynek's team led the work.
europmc-pmc3384466: Adult disease got a womb origin. This 2012 paper reviews how womb conditions shape adult disease. The authors map the origins. Their overview guides policy. Barouki's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped prenatal policy. The DOHaD field grew from it.
europmc-pmc3546866: Parkinson's got a stem-cell neuron study. This 2012 paper studies energy failure in PARK2 stem-cell neurons. The authors reveal the failure. Their work guides therapy. Imaizumi's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped Parkinson's models.
europmc-pmc3552766: Qualitative reviews got ENTREQ. This 2012 paper introduces ENTREQ for clearer qualitative reviews. The authors reveal the standard. Their work guides researchers. Tong's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Journals adopted the standard. The study shaped review standards.
europmc-pmc3552866: Alzheimer's got a neuron-loss study. This 2013 paper links mouse neuron loss to amyloid buildup. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides therapy. Eimer's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped Alzheimer's models.
europmc-pmc3555866: Mental disorders got a mortality study. This 2013 paper tracks excess deaths in 270,770 patients. The authors reveal the deaths. Their work guides policy. Nordentoft's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It shaped mental-health policy.
europmc-pmc3583166: Canada got an exercise-rules review. This 2010 review weighs the evidence behind Canada's exercise rules. The authors weigh the evidence. Their review guides policy. Warburton's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped fitness policy. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3594966: MAP kinase got a phosphatase review. This 2013 paper reviews dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatases. The authors map the shaping. Their review guides cell biology. Caunt's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3636866: PD-1 got a structure study. This 2013 paper maps the human PD-1 receptor shape. The authors reveal the interactions. Their work guides immunotherapy. Cheng's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc3645666: Plants got a backup-breathing review. This 2013 paper reviews alternative oxidase in plant stress. The author maps the pathway. Their review guides agriculture. Vanlerberghe's review is a classic. The paper is widely cited. It shaped crop science. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3715866: Tumors got a cell-line check. This 2013 paper checks if cell lines match real tumors. The authors reveal the match. Their work guides oncology. Domcke's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped cancer models.
europmc-pmc3796866: Back pain got a movement-therapy trial. This 2013 trial tests movement therapy for chronic back pain. The authors reveal the wins. Their work guides physiotherapy. Vibe Fersum's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3810466: Bacteria got PathogenFinder. This 2013 paper launches PathogenFinder to spot bad bugs. The authors reveal the tool. Their work guides microbiology. Cosentino's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It is open source. The study shaped pathogen detection.
europmc-pmc3821366: Muscles got a muscle-signal review. This 2013 paper reviews muscle-signal processing. The authors map the methods. Their review guides bioengineering. Chowdhury's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped prosthetics. The review is widely taught. Engineers rely on it.
europmc-pmc3833266: Weight got an every-other-day fast trial. This 2013 trial tests fasting every other day. The authors reveal the results. Their work guides nutrition. Varady's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped diet science.
europmc-pmc3838966: Photosynthesis got a battery-control review. This 2013 paper reviews battery control of photosynthesis. The authors map the control. Their review guides plant biology. Michelet's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped crop science. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3888466: Zika got a virus-family-tree study. This 2014 paper traces Zika's family tree. The authors reveal the tree. Their work guides virology. Faye's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped outbreak science. It is a landmark.
europmc-pmc3906566: Genes got a sponge-RNA review. This 2014 paper reviews sponge RNAs. The authors map the sponges. Their review guides genetics. Kartha's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped RNA science. The review is widely taught. Students rely on it.
