europmc-pmc3935566: Sugar got a Tre6P-hub review. This 2014 paper reviews sugar signaling via Tre6P. The authors map the hub. Their review guides botany. Yadav's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped plant science. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3958266: Gait got a how-you-walk gadgets review. This 2014 paper reviews walking-measurement gadgets. The authors map the gadgets. Their review guides rehab. Muro-de-la-Herran's review is widely cited. It is a classic. Clinics rely on it. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3966766: Mice got a run-away-fat study. This 2014 paper finds running reshapes fat mice's gut bugs. The authors reveal the reshaping. Their work guides nutrition. Evans's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped obesity science.
europmc-pmc3994566: Trials got a small-trial-stats question. This 2014 paper questions stats rules for small trials. The authors reveal the questioning. Their work guides biostatistics. Lee's paper is widely cited. It is a classic. Researchers rely on it. It is widely taught.

Their 2026 arXiv paper supports interactive information retrieval, the study of search as a back-and-forth process. The data pairs detailed interaction logs with facts about each searcher.

The logs cover 61 participants in 122 sessions. Alongside the clicks, the dataset records traits such as perceptual speed, topic interest, search skill, and basic demographics. Because the platform logs new sessions in the same format, other teams can extend the data. That makes user behavior in search easier to compare across studies.
arxiv-2601-09466: Dietrich Burde classifies the second cohomology spaces of filiform nilpotent Lie algebras. His 2026 arXiv paper covers all such algebras of dimension up to eleven over a field. For higher dimensions it handles certain classes. Filiform algebras are the most nilpotent ones of their size, stretched as far from abelian as possible. Cohomology spaces like these govern how an algebra can be extended. A full list for small dimensions gives other researchers firm ground to build on.
arxiv-2601-09566:
Shuyang Xiang and Hao Guan test whether language models can read Chinese characters as pictures. Their 2026 arXiv paper feeds low-resolution images of characters into a model as visual tokens. Standard models treat each character as an index in a list, ignoring its drawn form.

For a logographic script, the drawn form carries meaning and sound cues. The authors ask whether even coarse visual input can help character-level modeling. A hot start from pixels could ground the model in how characters are built. If vision helps, models for Chinese and similar scripts could lean less on arbitrary index tables.
arxiv-2601-09966:
Ruoxi Jia and co authors argue that the AI data trade is not fair. Data made by people feeds each step of model work. Raw text trains the model. The model then makes new text of its own. At each step, the data gets more refined.

Yet the pay and credit do not flow back. The team calls this a data deal gap. Those who make the data lose share as its worth grows. The paper says a sound AI trade needs deals that work for the makers. It sets out why the gap forms. It also frames what a fair deal must do.
arxiv-2601-10066:
Awanish Pandey gives a shape based way to move states in full. The work deals with pairs of modes that can trade states. A fixed gap in their tones blocks a full trade. Past fixes could not beat that block in full.

Pandey recasts the trade as a path on a sphere. The sphere is the Bloch sphere. Steps of matched phase move the state along the path. This view shows a cone near the goal that no path can cross. It also gives exact path rules for a full trade. The rules hold for a range of gaps, in both classic and quantum rigs.
arxiv-2601-10166:
Miriam Goldack, Yosi Atia, Ori Alberton, and Karl Jansen read flow facts off a quantum chip. Quantum tools may speed up flow sims a lot. A flow field can be packed into few qubits. Each qubit doubles the points it can hold. But the gain is lost if read out is slow.

Read out has had scant past work. The team test ways to pull stats from a flow state on real chips. Stats such as means and spreads are what flow work needs. They ask which read plans work on the chips of today. The work fills a gap in the quantum flow chain.
arxiv-2601-10366:
Bidisha Bhatt and Andreas Carlson study drops of fluid held in a soft spring. Springs show up in tools and in life forms. A soft spring bends with ease. At small scale, the skin of a fluid can pull hard. That pull can bend the spring.

The team ran tests with drops in such a spring. The drops take odd shapes. One is a ring. One is a grub like form. One is a ball. The shape rests on the pull of the fluid skin and the bend of the spring. The work maps when each shape forms.
arxiv-2601-10966:
Takeshi Fukuyama clarifies the role of trilinear kernels in integrable systems and in gravity. The Yu-Toda-Fukuyama trilinear equation is the anchor. Fukuyama shows it is not one evolution equation among many. It is one kernel that generates the whole hierarchy in three space dimensions plus time, once matching flows are picked.

He also shows the kernel at work in the gravity of spinning bodies. The same structure thus spans soliton math and spinning space. Universal kernels are prized: one object, many equations. The paper helps researchers see scattered results as outputs of a single machine, and may let gravity borrow tools built for integrable waves.
arxiv-2601-11066:
Hirosuke Yamamoto proposes an asymmetric encoding-decoding scheme for lossless data compression. Lossless schemes squeeze data so it can be restored exactly. The new scheme generalizes tANS, the tabled variant of asymmetric numeral systems, a modern coding family used in real compressors. In Yamamoto's scheme, the data sequence is encoded in backward order.

Decoding then proceeds in forward order, first symbol to last. Splitting the directions lets encoder and decoder each work in the order that suits them. Asymmetry here is a feature: encoding can be costly while decoding stays fast, or the reverse. The work serves compression theorists extending the ANS family that now powers many production codecs.
arxiv-2601-11166:
Artem E. Shitikov and co-authors measure optical losses in pure crystalline silicon in the infrared. The purest silicon, made for semiconductor technology, shows low absorption in the infrared. It now serves photonics in the telecom band, including high-Q whispering gallery mode microresonators. At longer wavelengths, the loss mechanisms are still not well studied.

The team uses those microresonators as exquisitely sensitive loss meters. A resonator's ring-down betrays even faint absorption. Knowing where losses rise tells designers which wavelengths silicon photonics can serve. The work matters for sensors, clocks, and quantum devices that plan to use silicon's purity beyond the telecom window.
arxiv-2601-09866:
Kiarie Ndegwa and eight co-authors estimate forest canopy height from ordinary satellite images. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents the team's new method, a generative super-resolution framework. It produces canopy height models at half-meter detail from Sentinel-2 imagery taken at ten-meter resolution.

Methods based on aerial photos are limited by rare, irregular flights. Sentinel-2 revisits the whole Earth on a steady schedule, so seasonal composites are always available. the team's new method uses flow matching to sharpen those images into height maps. Regular, fine canopy maps support carbon accounting and forest care across the world. They also give ground teams a cheap way to spot loss early, long before a site visit could be planned.
arxiv-2601-11366:
J. Manley and seven coauthors build tiny torsion pendulums for gravity tests. Their 2026 preprint reports nanofabricated devices for the bench. Lab-scale measures of gravity are a standing hard task. They are a gate to tests of quantum gravity ideas.

Torsion balances lead the field for tabletop gravity work. A hanging mass twists under the faint pull of a near mass. Thermal decoherence sets the main limit on such devices. Small, well-made pendulums can cut noise and size at once. Nanofabrication gives fine control of the pendulum's form. The team's devices aim at sharper tabletop tests. Such tests probe gravity where it is least understood.
arxiv-2601-11566:
Gurkirat Wadhwa and Priyank Sinha study stability of opportunistic supply chains. Their 2026 preprint appears in a European operations journal. Even giant firms face persistent swings in their inputs. Walmart, Apple, and Coca-Cola are named as cases.

Costs, demand, and raw material supply all fluctuate often. These are not rare shocks but sustained volatility. Classic disruption models target infrequent events and miss this. Under steady swings, firms act opportunistically with partners. They reconfigure ties often, with no long-term contracts. Trust deficits help drive that restless switching. The team analyzes when such chains stay stable as networks grow.
arxiv-2601-11666:
Muhammad Imran, Chi Lee, and Yugyung Lee make medical vision models explainable. Their 2026 preprint introduces MATEX, a framework for that task. Medical vision-language models read scans and text together. Clinicians need to know why such a model flags a region.

MATEX joins three techniques for sharper explanation maps. Multi-layer attention rollout tracks where the model looks. Text-guided spatial priors steer maps with clinical wording. Layer consistency analysis checks that maps stay stable. The result is gradient attribution maps with anatomy in mind. Precise, stable maps are more meaningful for clinicians. Trust in medical AI rests on such clear evidence.
arxiv-2601-13366:
Giulia Meucci and a large team find built in odd charge hubs in free films of a famed oxide pair. The pair joins LaAlO3 on SrTiO3. Their join hosts rich acts, such as odd pair of electrons in dots that acts as if charge cost were negative. That is a negative U hub.

In past work such hubs came from dots cut by design. Here the films are free membranes, peeled from a base. Hubs form on their own, since side bind comes from the film's own plan, not from cut walls. That ease of form may help teams study and use the effect. For quantum stuff teams, a built in hub beats a carved one.
arxiv-2601-13466:
Pedro Oliveira and co-authors draw lessons from a governance reform in the data.table open source project. The project is a high speed R package used in firm data work at scale. Like many open projects, it faced risk from loose or one person rule. One person rule strains as a user base grows.

A community led reform spread the rule to fix scale and long life risks. The paper is a case study of that shift. It tracks what drove the change and what it cost. For other open teams at the same wall, a worked case with names and dates beats a vague plea to reform.
arxiv-2601-12466:
S. Thatikonda and five co authors simulate how plasmoids form in a thin sheet of plasma current. A plasmoid is a blob of plasma pinched off from the sheet. Two instabilities compete to shape that process. One is the Kelvin Helmholtz instability, driven by shear flow. The other is the lower hybrid drift instability, driven by drifts across the sheet.

The team study the nonlinear stage in two dimensions, at low electron beta. They use a hybrid method that mixes kinetic and gyrokinetic simulation. That mix lets ions and electrons each get a fit treatment. The interplay of the two instabilities decides when blobs form and how they grow. Results here bear on magnetic reconnection in space and lab plasmas.
arxiv-2601-13766:
K. Zhao reports the expected reach of a dark matter hunt called BULLKID-DM in 2026. The quarry is light WIMP-like particles, with mass near one GeV or below. Such light dark matter is hard to catch with classic detectors. Their odds of hitting a nucleus must be below a very small bound.

The detector stacks diced silicon wafers as particle absorbers. Multiplexed kinetic inductance detectors sense the tiny hits. Projected sensitivity tells funders and teams what the hunt could find. A clear reach map guides the build and the later search.
arxiv-2601-14566:
Shenghan Gao and seven co-authors build a supply chain tool in this 2026 paper, set for the Intelligent User Interfaces conference. Supply chains are complex networks that span from raw material acquisition to product delivery, with enterprises as interconnected nodes. They play a pivotal role in organizational success. Optimizing them stays challenging, though.

Partner selection is a key bottleneck, shaped by both competitive and cooperative dynamics. The team's framework, SCSimulator, is an exploratory visual analytics system for that choice. It runs LLM-driven multi-agent simulation, so candidate partners can be tested in a virtual market first. Readers get a way to explore partner choices before signing real contracts.
arxiv-2601-15466:
Jana Franceska Funke, Ria Matapurkar, Enrico Rukzio, and Teresa Hirzle study avatars in virtual workouts in a 2026 arXiv paper. Virtual reality lets people shape their avatars as they wish. A user may pick a muscular body or a slim one. Such choices may change how people act with each other. That matters most in exercise settings, the authors note. There, body shape can signal athletic skill.

The study looks at three things at once. It asks how avatar shape and social context affect relatedness between users. It asks how they affect emotions during the workout. And it asks how they affect performance. The findings matter for VR design. Small choices about bodies on screen may shape how a group session feels and works.
arxiv-2601-15566:
Fan Yang and four co-authors add rigor to the study of protein change in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their data are sets of aligned protein sequences. Such sets play a key role in the study of how proteins change over time. One main use is contact prediction: guessing which parts of a protein touch. Most past methods rest on models or fixed rules. They rarely state how sure their predictions are.

The authors pursue model-free inference instead, per the title. They view protein change through the lens of coevolution. Sites that change together hint at contact in the folded shape. Inference with honest bounds helps users judge which calls to trust. A call with a range beats a bare yes or no. For protein science, that honesty can guide costly lab work.
arxiv-2601-15666:
Keito Uehara and Taichi Murayama study a new kind of harmful account on X in a 2026 arXiv paper. Impression zombies are accounts built to inflate engagement metrics. They flood the platform with low-quality, irrelevant posts. That flood degrades the experience for real users. The accounts have recently emerged as a significant threat on the service formerly called Twitter. The authors set two goals.

First, they measure the accounts' behavioral patterns in quantitative terms. Second, they build a method to detect such accounts. Detection is the practical payoff. Platforms need signals that separate zombie farms from genuine, if noisy, users. Honest metrics matter to advertisers and researchers alike. A reliable classifier helps clean the numbers everyone relies on.
arxiv-2601-15866:
Feng-Yuan Kuang, Lin Li, and Weibin Li study atom chains with paired excitations in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is a Rydberg atom chain. They focus on antiferromagnetic dimers inside it. A dimer is a bound pair of excitations. The regime of interest sets laser detuning to offset nearest-neighbor interactions. In that regime, an effective PXQ model describes the physics.

The authors show the Hilbert space splits apart. It decomposes into disconnected subspaces that each conserve dimers. They classify those subspaces and identify their basis states. A conserved dimer count simplifies the dynamics greatly. Rydberg chains are leading platforms for quantum simulation. Knowing their hidden conservation laws helps predict what they will do in experiments.
arxiv-2601-15066:
A. W. Romero Jorge, L. Sagunski, and co-authors gather limits on a particle that may not exist. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with dark photons, a dark sector particle tied to a new force. It links weakly to the standard model through kinetic mixing.

No single test can pin such a particle down. The team combines bounds from three fronts. High-energy collisions give one set of limits. Cosmology gives a second set, and astrophysics a third. Put together, the bounds narrow the space where a dark photon could still be hiding today.
arxiv-2601-16066:
Ju Gao and Fang Shen show a twist in the flow of a lone Dirac electron. Their 2026 preprint works in basic quantum theory. A Dirac electron with spin moves through space. The pair show it bears a real space flow that winds like a screw. This holds even with no swirl of the path as a whole.

The proof uses exact states for an electron held in a tube. The wound flow has a clear hand, left or right. It lasts into zones where the wave fades out. Its pitch is set by shape, not by the wave length of the move. The pair also link this flow to chiral fields near the path.
arxiv-2601-16266:
Andrea Caprotti, Joshua Morris and Borivoje Dakić study free choice in shadow sums. Their 2026 preprint deals with shadow tomography, a way to learn state traits from few reads. Rich read sets give more traits than the least set can. They also leave a pure classic free choice in the rebuild. The same trait can be built in end less ways from the same data.

The team seeks the best choice for a set task. Best means the least noise in the trait read from data. A good post step can lift gains with no new reads. That gain is free in gear terms and pure in code. The work sharpens a cheap step in quantum reads.
arxiv-2601-16466:
Jivnesh Sandhan and coauthors break model roles with set self cues. Their 2026 preprint deals with roles that models must hold firm. Roles count in schools, mind help and user aid work. A role that drifts can give bad or unsafe text. Past work stressed tale play roles, not firm work roles.

Foe chats push models to drop or swap their set role. The team tests how oft such pushes win in work roles. Win rates show which roles need more guard in build. Guards must hold the role but not block true help. The work maps a risk that grows with role use.
arxiv-2601-16666:
Chengyu Han, Qian Kong, Ming Shen, and Xi Chen study short pulses of light in glass fibers. Some pulses keep their shape as they race along. These pure-quartic pulses rest on a rare kind of spread in the fiber. Their 2026 preprint asks how to squeeze such pulses fast. A tighter pulse can carry more in less time.

The team looks at slow squeezes and quick ones. Quick routes use tricks that skip the slow path. Gain and loss along the fiber enter their math as well. The goal is a sharp pulse with no break-up. Such pulses could serve fast links and fine tools. The work maps safe ways to reach that goal.
arxiv-2601-16866:
Lucía Güitta-López, Vincenzo Suriani, Jaime Boal, Álvaro López-López, and Daniele Nardi help robot arms learn with less trial. Deep reward learning can master hard arm tasks. But it needs huge counts of tries to learn. Each try costs time, power, and wear. Their 2026 preprint adds word-based sense to cut that count.

Sense tags tell the arm what things are and how they link. Those tags guide the hunt for good moves. The arm then wastes fewer tries on blind paths. Less trial means labs can train arms in days, not weeks. It also cuts risk when arms learn near folks.
arxiv-2601-17166:
Amandip Sangha rebuilds a space's shape from how heat spreads in it. A spread rule on a space hides its full shape. His 2026 preprint pulls that shape from the rule's own acts. The rule is a symmetric spread semigroup, kept local. First and next step spread marks come from it. From those marks, the full weighted shape falls out.

No map of the space is gave in at the start. Shape here spans length, bend, and mass spread. Such gains join chance work to pure shape math. They may aid tools that learn shape from flows.
arxiv-2601-17466:
Peter Davidson and Michael Grinfeld propose a new measure of beta-diversity in ecology. Beta-diversity tracks how species mixes differ across sites. Their measure uses the energy of a graph sheaf Laplacian built from sample data. That scalar is easy to compute with basic linear algebra. Simple cases show its worth.

The authors say the new energy tells more than accepted measures. A richer signal helps ecologists see real change, not noise. Land and climate shifts show up first in mix changes. A cheap, sharp measure can run on large surveys with ease. The work gives field teams a tool that fits daily data. It may sharpen how change is tracked.
arxiv-2601-17566:
Qi Li and Xinchao Wang expose a stealth attack on tool-using AI agents. Tools let models solve hard tasks with high utility. Plug-and-play tool use is a draw for builders. The authors show the tool-calling process can be manipulated. Their Sponge Tool Attack is a denial-of-efficiency attack. It does not need to break the answer. It drains speed and resources instead.

Slow agents cost money and can fail time-bound jobs. A stealth drain is hard to spot in logs. The work warns that efficiency is a security trait. Defenses must watch tool call patterns, not just outputs. As agents gain tools, their attack surface grows. This study maps one quiet corner of it.
arxiv-2601-17666:
Xinyue Pan, Yuhao Chen, and Fengqing Zhu generate multi-food images without training. Real meal photos hold many food items at once. Dietary assessment uses such images to judge intake. Recipe tools use them to show finished dishes. Diffusion models struggle with multi-food scenes. Adjacent foods blend into each other, a flaw called object entanglement.

Their training-free method uses prompt grafting. Grafting joins prompts so each food keeps its place. Clean multi-food images can augment scarce datasets. That helps diet apps learn from fewer real photos. The work targets a niche where errors are easy to spot. A plate with merged foods fools no one.
arxiv-2601-17766: David Kurniadi Angdinata studies how to compute L-functions for a class of representations over global function fields. The 2026 preprint treats representations that are unramified at almost every place. Their L-functions are known to be rational in a set variable and to obey a functional equation up to a sign. The paper gives ways to pin down both the function and that sign by computation.
arxiv-2601-17966:
Naman Gupta and co-authors ask how technology researchers can help in the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous relatives. Their 2026 preprint addresses North America, called Turtle Island by many Indigenous peoples. Indigenous people face far higher rates of disappearance and murder. The authors describe the crisis as rooted in settler-colonial violence and systemic erasure. Technology plays a double role in that harm.

Tools can impede searches and spread harm. They can also power advocacy and resistance. The paper draws lessons for researchers who build search, data, and safety tools. It urges work that stands with Indigenous communities rather than studying them from outside. The stakes are lives, not just data.
arxiv-2601-18066:
Gabriel K. Kruell and co-authors look for hidden math in ancient Mesoamerican design. Their 2026 preprint studies calendars and monumental buildings. Understanding how these societies wove math into design needs care for their own ways of knowing. Text proof for values like the golden ratio or pi is scarce. The authors test whether rational approximations that fit those constants appear in calendrics and architecture in a steady way.

They also stress astronomical dualities, paired patterns in sky watching. If the ratios hold up under fair tests, they hint at shared design rules. If not, the field learns to drop a tempting myth. Either way, the work models how to test claims about ancient math with respect.
arxiv-2601-18866:
Emily Mader and eight co-authors test two big model sets against the smallest stars and brown dwarfs. These ultracool dwarfs are dim and cool, so their spectra must be matched to models to learn their heat and makeup. The team grades two cloudy model grids on low resolution near infrared spectra.

One grid is Sonora Diamondback and the other is an older set by Saumon and Marley. Each is fit to hundreds of objects that span late M, L, and T types. A fair grade of both grids shows observers which one to trust, and where each still misses the real sky.
arxiv-2601-19066:
Runxiang Cheng and seven co-authors make repair agents write the failing test along with the fix. In agentic program repair, a bug reproduction test proves a bug is real and checks that a patch kills it. Human developers often write that test beside their fix, and the team found agent users want the same.

Their method grows the test and the fix together, each feeding the other as the agent works. A patch that ships with its own proof test earns more trust from reviewers. The work comes from real deployment of repair agents, where such trust decides whether patches get merged.
arxiv-2601-19166:
Andrew N. Glaudell and five co-authors build exact quantum circuits for two qubits with the fewest costly gates. Exact synthesis promises the best possible circuit and a standard form, but it has been stuck in small, narrow corners. Their framework works over the Clifford plus T gate set and optimizes the T count exactly.

T gates are the pricey part of fault tolerant quantum computing, so cutting them cuts real cost. A method that proves its count is the true minimum gives compiler builders a firm target. Two qubit blocks sit inside nearly every larger circuit, so gains here echo widely.
arxiv-2601-19466:
Richard Mandel, Corto Mascle, and Georg Zetzsche work in formal language theory, the mathematics of grammars and machines. Indexed languages are a classic class in this field. They are exactly the languages accepted by a kind of stacked machine used in checking higher-order programs. The downward closure of a language collects all the scattered subwords of its words.

That closure is known to be a regular language, a simpler object that approximates the original. The authors study how complex it is to compute and describe this closure. Questions like this test the border between what machines can and cannot decide. They also matter for program checking, where over-approximations must stay cheap. The paper pins down the cost of this closure for indexed languages.
arxiv-2601-19666:
Josh Givens, Song Liu, Henry W. J. Reeve, and Katarzyna Reluga work on measuring how treatments affect different people. Averages can hide the fact that a treatment helps some patients and not others. Quantile-based measures look at effects across the outcome range, not just at the mean. A newer summary, the conditional quantile comparator, keeps quantile detail while staying fairly interpretable.

The authors develop a direct doubly robust estimator for these quantile contrasts. Doubly robust methods stay valid if one of two working models is right. Direct estimation targets the contrast itself rather than building it from pieces. Better estimators mean trials can report fairer, more detailed effects. The work serves clinical and policy studies where who benefits matters as much as whether it works.
arxiv-2601-19766:
Allyson Hahn and Krishnan Raghavan study how a neural network's architecture shapes continual learning. Models with fixed architecture struggle when data distributions shift from task to task. The authors build a mathematical framework that treats architecture and weights together. Both live in a Sobolev space, a setting that tracks smoothness.

Within that framework they can rigorously ask how architecture affects the forgetting loss. Forgetting is the drop in performance on old tasks as new ones are learned. If architecture itself drives part of the forgetting, design choices become a lever against it. The work gives theory to a question usually settled by trial and error. It may guide networks that grow or reshape as tasks arrive.
arxiv-2601-19866:
Manuel Cavieres, Sergey E. Koposov, Elena Maria Rossi, and colleagues report a star fleeing the centre of our galaxy. Hypervelocity stars are thrown out by tidal encounters with the central supermassive black hole. Born near that black hole, they gain enough speed to escape the galactic centre. They can then be spotted far out in the galactic halo.

The team found such a star in data from the DESI survey's first release. Each confirmed escapee is a probe of the black hole's surroundings. Their speeds and paths record the violent dynamics near the centre. They also test gravity in an extreme setting. The discovery adds a rare member to a small known class.
arxiv-2601-19966:
Jonas Elsborg and five colleagues predict the electron charge density of crystals with a fast neural model. Charge density is a fundamental property that determines how a material behaves. Computing it with traditional quantum methods is slow. Their model, ELECTRAFI, builds the density from anisotropic Gaussians placed in real space.

The trick is mathematical: Gaussians have closed-form Fourier transforms. Using the Poisson summation formula, the model evaluates plane-wave coefficients analytically. That makes the whole model differentiable end to end and fast. Accurate, quick charge densities would speed materials screening for batteries and catalysts. The work shows how classical harmonic analysis can sharpen modern machine learning. The trick is neat and fast. It turns a hard sum into a short one. That speed is the whole point of the work.
arxiv-2601-20066:
Darren Dahunsi and colleagues present a new ultrasound imaging method for seeing inside the body in three dimensions. High-quality volumetric imaging is hard with today's probes. Matrix probes have limited fields of view and element counts. Row-column arrays offer an alternative geometry but bring their own compromises.

Their method, OPTIMUS, transmits and receives orthogonal plane waves with isotropic focusing. It uses row-column arrays whose bias can be switched to steer the imaging. The goal is structural volume images with wide coverage and fine detail. Better bedside volumetric imaging would aid diagnosis without moving patients to large scanners. The work pushes array design and beamforming together.
arxiv-2601-20466:
Mathis Brossier and ten colleagues design and evaluate an AI pilot for planetarium shows in science centers. The pilot works inside OpenSpace, a visualization tool for space data, during live public events. The piloting role is usually held by a human who works in close partnership with the guide on stage.

The team studies how a language model can take the pilot's seat, flying the view while the presenter talks. Live shows cannot pause for errors, so the pilot must respond fast and stay on script. A capable AI pilot could free presenters to focus on the audience.
arxiv-2601-18366:
Celia Álvarez Álvarez and Mariamo Mussa Juane test a core rule of quantum theory on a real quantum machine. The rule, from Niels Bohr, says a thing can act like a wave or like a bit of stuff. The two views do not show at once. A fresh form of the rule ties the two views in one neat link.

The pair ran two tests built on tools that split and join beams of light. One test used a lone quantum bit, and the next used two bits linked as a pair. Both tests ran on true hardware, not on a mock up. Results from real chips show how far the rule holds when noise and flaws creep in. Such checks help turn a grand claim of old theory into hard fact that labs can use.
arxiv-2601-18466:
Dumiso Mithi and three colleagues use the maths of change to study how the large web of galaxies grows. They look at the dark side of space, where dark power and dark matter may trade push and pull. Two forms of that trade are tried, one straight and one curved. The dark power in their setup comes from a ghost field in the theory of the strong force.

Tools from the maths of change let them find the calm points of the setup. At a calm point the web can sit or drift in a set way for a long time. The team check which calm points hold firm and which ones match the growth we see. Such work helps sort which dark plans can match the real sky. It also shows which plans fail on math grounds alone.
arxiv-2601-18566:
Fabio Massacci and Winnie Bahati Mbaka call for a deep change in how a top software meet shares new work. They blame the plain paper for two ills: a chase for new-ness at all costs, and a crisis in which finds cannot be run again to check them. Each ill feeds the next, they say. Fresh claims win space, while checks and re-runs get short shrift.

Their plan swaps the plain paper for a two-tier path. First comes a short plan, shared and judged on its worth as a plan. Then comes a report of what the work found, judged on how well it kept to the plan. The pair build on a form of report that some fields use now. A shift like this could reward care over flash in software work.
arxiv-2601-18766:
A study takes on a gap in tools that name the mode of a piece of Indian art music. Each such piece is built on a raga, a set of notes and moves that give the piece its mood. There are far more ragas than tapes to train on. A few are played a lot, and a long tail is played so rare that no tape of them sits in the training set at all.

A plain sorter can only name ragas it has seen. It fails on the tail, and it cannot even group the rare ones in a sane way. The new frame aims to learn new ragas as they come, with no loss of the old ones. That skill, to learn and not forget, is key for a live art with a long tail. It could serve archives that hold vast sets of tapes with thin tags.
arxiv-2601-21166:
Taha El Bakkali, Rayane Bouftini, Qiuyi Zhang, and Omar Saadi tackle a hard search problem where only rough pairwise comparisons are available. The goal is to lower a smooth but bumpy cost function in many dimensions. Older methods that use no gradients are held back by the full size of the space.

The authors propose a direct search method built on random line searches. It adjusts itself to the true low size of the problem rather than the full space. That shift matters when most directions barely change the cost. The method offers a way to optimize when exact scores cannot be trusted or measured.
arxiv-2601-21266:
Zhuochen Liu, Hans Walker, and Rahul Jain compare neural networks with classic filters for tracking the hidden state of a system. Filters used in control rely on known equations for how a system moves and how noisy it is. Neural models can instead learn the job from data alone.

The study asks how far the learned models act like true filters in systems that do not move in straight lines. That question matters for control and for choices made under uncertainty. If a network only mimics answers on test data, it may fail when conditions shift. The comparison shows where each approach can be trusted.
arxiv-2601-21566:
Suresh Govindarajan, Sreehari A Padinhareveettil, and Raghotham A Kulkarni compute entanglement measures for fields living in curved space. Entanglement entropy and negativity gauge how strongly two regions of a field are linked. Classic calculations covered flat space and simple fields.

The authors extend the numbers to scalar and gauge fields in curved settings. They lay space out on a grid in a way that respects the curvature. Their results are then checked against predictions from heat kernel methods. Reliable numbers help test ideas about black holes and the early universe, where curvature is the whole point.
arxiv-2601-21666:
Ahmed Y. Radwan, Christos Emmanouildis, Hina Tabassum, Deval Pandya, and Shaina Raza present a real-world benchmark for audio-video understanding in large multimodal models. Most earlier tests used still images. Live scenes, though, unfold over time with sound and motion together.

Their benchmark, SONIC-O1, grades models on sequential audio-video data drawn from real settings. It checks whether models can follow events as they develop, not just label a frame. Sound carries cues that vision alone misses, from alarms to tone of voice. A shared real-world test helps the field see which models truly follow a scene.
arxiv-2601-22266:
Mainak Mukhopadhyay and Shigeo Kimura chase the source of one extreme neutrino seen in the sea. A deep sea detector in the Mediterranean caught a particle with huge energy in 2023. Their 2026 preprint asks if a class of bright flashes, driven by pulsars, could be the source.

They study the summed glow of neutrinos such flashes would send out as a group. Then they test whether that glow could yield one event like the one seen. The work links a single rare catch to a whole class of cosmic events. It helps teams judge where such particles are born.
arxiv-2601-22366:
Michael Dritschel, Alejandra Maestripieri, and James Rovnyak define gauges of plus and minus for operators on a Kreĭn space. Such a space tracks a form that can take both signs, unlike a plain inner product. Their 2026 preprint studies self-adjoint operators, which match their own adjoint, on these spaces.

The gauges, called Hermitian indices, read as shape-based counts of the plus and minus parts. The team then split the operator into clean factors tied to those counts. The work is pure math, in operator theory. It gives peers a sharp new set of terms. Later work can build on the split.
arxiv-2601-22666:
Junyi Hu and five co-authors ground phrases in images under weak guidance, led by what the model expects. Open-vocabulary grounding links free text to the right image region, for classes never named in training. Their 2026 preprint, ExpAlign, notes that past tools use blunt whole-sentence codes or heavy, supervised token links.

Their frame aligns vision and language through confidence-based teaching, with a firm theory base. Sharper grounding helps search, robotics, and access tools. The work seeks fine links without fine labels. That trade is the hard part, and the point.
arxiv-2601-21766:
Amit Dhurandhar and co-authors look for an alternative to the Transformer for generating language. Transformers are the default architecture for this task, but the team takes inspiration from a classic math object. Continued fractions, where a value is built from nested layers of simpler parts.

Their 2026 preprint introduces a new family of functions for generative modeling, and the networks that implement it, called CoFrGeNets. The idea is to see whether this nested structure can produce language with different strengths or costs than attention-based models. Work of this kind matters because nearly all modern language systems share one design, so a credible second family would widen the field's options considerably.
arxiv-2601-21866:
Evandro Ortigossa, Guy Lutsker, and Eran Segal work on forecasting long stretches of multivariate time series. Real series mix global trends, local cycles, and regimes that shift without warning, which makes long-horizon prediction hard. Mixture-of-experts models help by letting specialist sub-networks handle different patterns.

Most such models, though, build every expert the same way, from identical simple blocks. Those uniform experts capture diverse time patterns poorly. The team's 2026 preprint, MoHETS, uses a mixture of heterogeneous experts, specialists with different designs suited to different dynamics. Better long-range forecasts feed planning in energy, logistics, and finance, where decisions must be made weeks ahead on the strength of today's data.
arxiv-2601-21966:
Sebastian Peters and co-authors work on securing the communication buses inside cyber-physical systems. These systems link embedded devices in cars, factories, and machines. Messages on their buses need integrity and authenticity, which usually means a shared group key for message authentication codes.

Fixed pre-shared keys are insecure, and trusting keys on first use is not much better. A group key agreement protocol lets devices establish fresh shared keys together. The team's 2026 preprint develops such agreement for system buses. Getting key agreement onto constrained bus hardware matters because these networks steer physical processes, where a forged message can break equipment or hurt people.
arxiv-2601-22166:
Roberto Garrone helps owners decide what a failing property should become. A growing share of the building stock underperforms persistently, for reasons that cycles and poor maintenance no longer explain. Some assets sit in good locations, technically recoverable, yet fail to earn what their tied-up capital should.

Choosing a new use for such a site is a decision under deep uncertainty. Garrone's 2026 preprint builds a multi-criteria framework that is aware of real options, the value of keeping future choices open. Redevelopment choices lock in capital for decades, so a framework that prices flexibility alongside rent and cost speaks directly to investors and city planners.
arxiv-2601-20866:
Huiguang Zhang analyzes the accuracy limits of a method for reading signals sampled too slowly. The 2026 paper concerns the synchronous Nyquist-folding generalized eigenvalue method, or SNGEM. The method estimates frequency, amplitude, and phase for multi-tone signals. It works at extreme sub-Nyquist rates, far below the usual sampling rule. It does so by processing a signal together with its time derivative.

Zhang derives the exact Cramér-Rao bound for one key parameter. That bound is the lowest error any estimator can reach. The parameter is an amplitude ratio tied to the tone's frequency. The paper then checks how close SNGEM comes to that limit. Near-optimal performance would certify the method for hard sensing jobs. Such jobs include radar and spectrum monitoring with cheap, slow hardware.
arxiv-2601-20966:
Kylar Greene, Aurora Ireland, Gordan Krnjaic, and Yuhsin Tsai derive a universal spectrum for a class of cosmic signals. Their 2026 paper concerns B-modes in the cosmic microwave background. Many early universe scenarios predict tensor ripples from causal sources after inflation. These sources act below the horizon and for a bounded time. Their microphysics may differ wildly. Yet their spectra share a universal scaling at small wavenumber.

On super-horizon scales, the tensor power grows as the cube of the wavenumber. That is the signature of white noise at production time. Observers can thus test many theories with one template. The paper gives that template a firm basis. It pairs with data studies that set limits on such sources. Together they narrow how the early universe could have rung.
arxiv-2601-21066:
Kealan Dunnett and four co-authors craft stronger hidden attacks on object detectors. Their 2026 paper presents BadDet+, a backdoor attack framework. Backdoor attacks plant a secret trigger in a model. The model behaves normally until the trigger appears. Their impact on object detection remains poorly understood, compared with image classification. The authors identify critical weaknesses in existing detection-based attacks. Chief among them are unrealistic assumptions.

Many prior attacks also lack physical validation. A trigger that works only on a screen is a weak threat. BadDet+ aims for attacks that survive the real world. Stronger attacks are not just a danger; they are a measuring tool. Defenders need realistic threats to test their guards. The paper sharpens both sides of that contest.
arxiv-2512-00666:
L Voigt wrote a 2025 cosmology paper on weak lensing, the slight bending of light from far galaxies by matter in between. Measuring that bend, called shear, helps map dark matter and test models of the universe. New Stage IV surveys will measure shear with great care and detail.

Voigt focuses on a sneaky source of error. Galaxies too faint to be detected still add their light and can bias the shear values. Using a machine learning method built to avoid noise bias, the author measures that effect for a survey like Euclid. The results help planners keep faint galaxies from skewing their maps.
arxiv-2512-01166:
Lily Stelling and five coauthors evaluate the safety frameworks of frontier AI companies in a 2025 paper. After the AI Seoul Summit in 2024, twelve AI companies published frontier safety frameworks. These documents outline how each firm plans to manage catastrophic risks from advanced AI systems.

New laws increasingly treat the frameworks as accountability mechanisms and fold them into reporting duties. The authors ask what the frameworks actually commit each company to do. Comparing promises across firms shows where commitments are concrete and where they are vague. That clarity helps regulators and the public judge whether self-governance is real.
arxiv-2601-23066:
Xiaoxuan Guo and seven co-authors push audio language models to listen for real acoustic evidence. Speech deepfake detection asks whether a clip is genuine or machine-made. Audio models are strong on content, but their judgments lean on word meaning and can overlook fine acoustic artifacts.

Their approach presses the model to perceive explicit acoustic cues before deciding. Grounding the call in sound details, not semantics, should cut errors on tricky fakes. Better detectors matter as voice cloning spreads into fraud and media. Fine-grained acoustic artifacts are the evidence the method forces forward, because synthetic speech often betrays itself in small sound details.
arxiv-2601-23166:
Lan Zhang, Marco Valentino, and André Freitas improve autoformalization, the mapping of math into formal language. Statement-level mapping has advanced fast, but full theorems remain largely unexplored. Older rework loops fix one aspect at a time, such as syntax, and miss the joint picture.

Their monotonic, reference-free rework optimizes several quality dimensions together, without needing a gold reference. Full-theorem formalization would let proof assistants check real mathematics at scale. Steady joint improvement is a step toward libraries of machine-verified results. Full-theorem formalization is the frontier named, moving beyond the isolated statements that earlier rework loops handled.
arxiv-2512-00166:
Ultralight dark matter, if it exists, would push gently on ordinary objects with tiny oscillating forces. Louis Hamaide, Hannah Banks, Peter Barker, and Andrew Geraci propose a new sensor to detect those forces in 2025. Their design uses optically levitated objects held in place by light.

Optically trapped sensors are known for high force sensitivity but have been little explored for dark matter searches. The proposed tabletop experiment, called MOLeQuTE, is tunable to different force patterns. A positive signal would be a major discovery, and even a null result narrows the space of allowed dark matter models. Tabletop experiments are far cheaper than collider or space missions, which adds to the appeal.
arxiv-2512-00366:
Forecasting data that moves through space and time, like traffic or weather, usually needs heavy models. Wenshuo Wang, Yaomin Shen, Yingjie Tan, and Yihao Chen present a knowledge distillation method for it in 2025. Distillation trains a small student model to copy a large teacher.

Their method, named in the title with semantic and spectral parts, preserves both meaning and frequency structure. Recent frequency-aware distillation already showed that keeping high-frequency details and low-frequency trends matters. A faithful lightweight student could bring strong spatiotemporal forecasts to devices and services that cannot run the full teacher model. Spectral preservation keeps both the sudden spikes and the slow drifts of the data.
arxiv-2512-00566:
Shape-free regression lets the data choose the curve, but that freedom creates bias that ruins naive confidence ranges. Giuseppe Cavaliere and co-authors improve inference for nonparametric regression in 2025. Such estimators are central to the economist's toolkit, including regression-discontinuity designs.

Large-sample bias throws off the true coverage of standard intervals, so reported confidence is often false confidence. Existing robust bias-corrected intervals help, yet the authors push the theory further. Credible ranges matter wherever policy is judged by estimated effects at a cutoff, from education funding to health eligibility rules. Regression discontinuity is where these intervals are most often used in policy work. Improved inference means narrower honest intervals, not just corrected ones. For folks who judge aid or school rules by a line in the sand, the gain is trust. The spread they quote is the spread the data can back up in full.
arxiv-2512-03166:
Robot soccer is a tough test for teams of AI agents. Aya Taourirte and Md Sohag Mia study learning methods for that test in this 2025 work. Agents must decide in real time, work as a team, and cope with rivals in a virtual field.

Reinforcement learning is a promising route, but it strains under split tasks. Long-term plans and split-second moves need different handling, and many agents add complexity. The authors work on methods that scale better. Progress here could transfer to warehouse robots, rescue teams, and other real multi-agent jobs. Virtual soccer gives a safe, cheap arena to test team tactics before real robots play.
arxiv-2512-03366:
Judging an A/B test method is hard when true effects are unknown. Ryan Kessler, James McQueen, and Miikka Rokkanen offer a way around that in this 2025 work. They split each test's data into two parts to measure method performance.

Their framework shows sample-split estimators are generally biased for full-sample performance. Yet those estimators consistently estimate the sample-split analogues of it. Knowing that gap helps firms judge testing methods honestly. Better method checks lead to better product and policy decisions from experiments. Sample splits are cheap, since they reuse data that testing teams already collect.
arxiv-2512-03466:
Two agents with half the facts each must cooperate to win. Xavier Cadet, Edward Koh, and Peter Chin present AsymPuzl in this 2025 work. Most multi-agent setups use open-ended role-play, which is hard to evaluate in a controlled way.

AsymPuzl is a minimal two-agent puzzle with information asymmetry. Each agent sees a partial, complementary view of a symbolic puzzle. They must exchange messages to solve it together. The setup isolates communication skill, a clean target for testing language model teamwork. Minimal puzzles strip away role-play noise, leaving pure communication skill exposed.
arxiv-2512-02066:
Sorting breast tumor images into benign and malignant is a high-stakes classification task where better feature extraction could help. Ece Yurtseven's 2025 paper builds a hybrid quantum-classical convolutional network for the job, running several quantum circuits in parallel and fusing their features.

The network is tested on BreastMNIST, a standard benchmark of breast tumor images prepared for machine learning. Quantum machine learning promises richer ways to pull signal from high-dimensional medical data, though the hardware remains young. Testing parallel quantum circuits on a real diagnostic benchmark shows where the approach stands and what it might add to classical networks.
arxiv-2512-02366:
Quantum sensors measure temperature, fields, and time with precision bounded by a quantity called the quantum Fisher information. Rui Zhang and three co-authors derive in 2025 a universal upper bound on that quantity for probes in thermal equilibrium with their surroundings.

The work unifies the equilibrium and non-equilibrium frameworks of quantum metrology for many-body systems, under dynamic sensing schemes. A universal bound tells experimentalists the best any thermal probe could ever do, before they build it. Such limits discipline the search for quantum sensors that beat classical instruments in real, warm conditions.
arxiv-2512-02566:
Kun Yuan and nine co-authors train AI models that read medical figures and text together. Biomedical vision language models learn from web scale scientific papers. Most training, though, pairs a whole figure with its caption and drops the fine links between small regions and words.

Clinicians rely on exactly those fine links when they zoom into local structures. The team's zoom in pretraining keeps panel level detail, matching small figure regions with the text that describes them. Models trained this way could support diagnosis and research tools that point to the right spot, not just the right page. Fine links like these are what let a tool point to a spot, not just a page, when it counts.
arxiv-2512-02666:
Ashkan Abedi, Vittorio Giovannetti, and Dario De Santis simulate a classic model of electrons on a square lattice. The two dimensional Hubbard model captures how electrons hop and repel, a core puzzle in condensed matter. Tensor network methods must first flatten the square into a chain.

The team maps the lattice with a Hilbert curve, a space filling path that keeps nearby sites close. That compact mapping yields a smaller matrix product state than the usual snake path. Cheaper simulations let physicists probe larger systems in the search for new phases of matter. Flat maps that keep near sites near are a cheap win, and cheap wins stack up in long runs fast.
arxiv-2512-02766:
Yichao Huang, Jinglin Wang, and Xiaolin Zeng refine a lattice model used to probe disordered quantum systems. The model, known by its H 2|2 label, lives on a hierarchical lattice with a tree like structure. Earlier work by Disertori, Merkl, and Rolles gave an exact coarse graining for its random field.

The authors extend that result to the model's random Schrödinger operator form. They also build fine graining, the reverse move, and prove an exponential martingale property for it. Two way scaling tools help connect small scale randomness with large scale behavior in disordered media. Two way scale moves let a proof climb from the small to the large and back, a round trip few tools can make.
arxiv-2512-02966:
Isha Chaudhary and five co-authors build Lumos, a system for certifying language model systems against stated properties. As these systems spread into more applications, alignment with human ethics grows crucial. Recent works certify properties like fairness, correct answering, and safety, but each method is ad hoc.

Ad hoc certificates are hard to generalize from one property or model to the next. Lumos aims at certification as a reusable system, not a one off proof. Portable certification could give regulators and buyers a common way to check AI claims before deployment. One stamp for many traits beats ten stamps for ten traits. Shops must ship a tool that firms and boards can trust at scale in the field.
plos-pone-0010066:
The authors were Julia Arciero, G. Bard Ermentrout, Jeffrey Upperman, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE paper modeled a severe gut disease of premature babies. Necrotizing enterocolitis attacks the intestines of pre-term infants. It is thought to involve an immature gut and changed levels of normal gut bacteria.

Instead of lab animals, the team built a mathematical model of the disease. They used it to test how probiotics, helpful live bacteria, and inflammation interact. A working model lets doctors explore treatment ideas safely before trying them in fragile newborns. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.
plos-pone-0010166:
Clint Winkler, Alberto Ponce, and Albert Courey studied gene silencing in fruit flies in 2010. Their PLOS ONE paper covered Groucho, a corepressor that helps turn genes off. Groucho binds a partner enzyme, Rpd3, that removes acetyl tags from histones. Earlier cell studies suggested that binding was required for repression, but its role in living animals was less certain.

The team proposed that this partnership raises nucleosome density, packing DNA more tightly. Denser packing makes genes harder to read, reinforcing the off state. The work links a classic repressor to the physical layout of chromosomes.
plos-pone-0010266:
The authors were Germain Fernando, Xianfeng Chen, Tarl Prow, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study delivered flu vaccine through skin in mice. Over fourteen million people die yearly from infectious diseases despite wide vaccine use. Most vaccines still go in by needle into muscle, a device dating to 1853, though skin is rich in immune cells.

By micro-targeting vaccine precisely into skin, guided by probability models, they got potent immunity. Strong protection came from low doses that a needle might waste. Dose-sparing delivery could stretch vaccine supplies in a pandemic.
plos-pone-0010366:
John Nomellini and co-workers built a bacteria-based HIV blocker for PLOS ONE in 2010. Preventing HIV infection needs new tools, since early microbicide gels had mostly failed. Past gels acted in broad, non-specific ways. This team took a targeted route instead. They used a harmless water bacterium that coats itself in a protein layer.

The bacteria were engineered to display two human proteins on that outer layer. One, CD4, is the very handle HIV uses to enter cells. The other is a signal that can also interfere with the virus. Together they may trap or block HIV before it reaches real cells. A living, self-growing blocker would be cheap to make if it works.
plos-pone-0009866:
Building muscle in the embryo means making some proteins and clearing others on schedule. Yvan Campos and colleagues found an enzyme that clears a fetal muscle protein at the right time. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myosin is the protein that pulls muscle fibers tight.

The enzyme is Ozz-E3, a ubiquitin ligase that tags proteins for disposal. Its target is sarcomeric embryonic myosin heavy chain, a motor protein of young muscle. Tagging it during muscle development makes room for adult forms. The handoff shows how timed cleanup shapes growing tissue.
plos-pone-0009966:
During the 2009 pandemic, labs needed a test that could name the new flu virus fast. Martin Schulze and colleagues built a real-time PCR approach for exactly that. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The approach differentiates pandemic influenza A(H1N1)v from recent human influenza viruses. Real-time PCR counts viral genes as they multiply, giving answers in hours. A wrong call could mislead whole outbreak reports. Telling the pandemic strain from seasonal ones guided treatment and tracking. The method served labs while the pandemic was active. Hours, not days, decided care in the surge.
